links.label: Aviation Instructor’s Handbook — Teaching Methods / Flight Instruction

details.summary: Although not always required by regulation at that altitude, supplemental oxygen is recommended for night flight above about 5,000 feet — night vision is especially hypoxia-sensitive.

Altitude-chamber (or similar controlled hypoxia) training’s main advantage is that each pilot learns their own personal hypoxia symptoms in a safe, supervised setting. Symptom sets differ person-to-person; recognizing your pattern early is the teaching point — not merely watching others or relying on rapid chamber repressurization.

links.label: FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (aeromedical education)

details.summary: Hypemic (“anemic”) hypoxia occurs when blood cannot carry enough oxygen — classic classroom example is carbon monoxide from a leaking exhaust system binding to hemoglobin. Symptoms resemble hypoxic hypoxia, but the cause is blood oxygen transport, not low ambient pressure. Treat with fresh air / oxygen and land; fix the exhaust leak on the ground.
Effective traffic-pattern collision avoidance: maintain the proper pattern altitude and continually scan. Altitude discipline keeps you predictable; scanning finds traffic early.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Most midair collisions occur during daylight in VFR conditions — often on clear days near airports/traffic patterns where traffic density is high. See-and-avoid never stops just because the weather is “nice.”

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Most effective night traffic technique: avoid staring directly at the suspected aircraft — use peripheral / off-center vision and a scanning pattern. Staring bleaches night vision on that spot and can make the target disappear.

FAA definition: Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) is a systematic approach to the mental process used by pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances. It is more than “good judgment” alone — it is a structured process (DECIDE plus risk tools like PAVE/CARE).

Risk management within ADM reduces flight risk through situational awareness, problem recognition, and good judgment. Teach students to notice change early (SA), name the problem, then apply sound judgment and mitigation — not just memorize procedures after the fact.

One explicit step in the ADM process is identifying personal attitudes hazardous to safe flight. Before antidotes or DECIDE steps help, the pilot must know which hazardous attitude is driving the poor choice. Build this into debriefs: “Which attitude showed up today?”

Classic behavioral traps for experienced pilots: complete the flight as planned, please passengers, meet schedules, and “get the job done.” Call these out in ADM scenario training — mission completion pressure is a leading human-factor hazard.

Dangerous tendencies / behavior patterns called out in ADM training include peer pressure, get-there-itis / scud running, loss of situational awareness, and operating with inadequate fuel (or energy/options) reserves. Instructors should name these patterns in scenario training and require a mitigation before launch.

To get a realistic view of your attitude toward flying, take a Self-Assessment Hazardous Attitude Inventory Test (FAA ADM materials). It surfaces which of the five hazardous attitudes you lean toward so you can practice antidotes.

Classic hazardous attitudes include antiauthority (“don’t tell me”), impulsivity (“do it quickly”), and resignation (“what’s the use”) — along with macho and invulnerability. Know the five; this question samples three of them. Pair each with its antidote phrase in oral prep.

Hazardous attitudes are counteracted by an appropriate antidotal phrase (e.g., antiauthority → “Follow the rules. They are usually right.”; impulsivity → “Not so fast. Think first.”; invulnerability → “It could happen to me.”; macho → “Taking chances is foolish.”; resignation → “I’m not helpless. I can make a difference.”). Recognition alone is not enough — apply the antidote.

The five hazardous attitudes every pilot faces to some degree: antiauthority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation. Memorize all five and their antidotes for the FOI/ADM oral and written.

The first step in neutralizing a hazardous attitude is recognizing the hazardous thought when it appears. Only after recognition can the pilot apply the antidote and choose a safer action. Drill recognition in flight debriefs with concrete examples from the lesson.

When you recognize a hazardous thought: label it as hazardous, then correct it by stating the corresponding antidotal phrase — and act on the antidote. Recognition without the antidote leaves the bad attitude in charge.

Hazardous attitude — anti-authority: “The aircraft can handle a lot more than maneuvering speed.” Va (or design maneuvering speed) is a structural/control limit in turbulence and abrupt inputs; instructors must model respect for it, not dismiss it.
Antidote for the macho hazardous attitude (“I can do it / watch this”): “Taking chances is foolish.” Pair recognition with the antidote phrase, then choose the safer action.

Cockpit stress management starts before the crisis: assess stress areas in one’s personal life. Life stress carries into the cockpit and reduces spare mental capacity. Instructors should model go/no-go honesty when life stress is high (IMSAFE: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating).

At the first sign of cockpit stress, relax and think rationally — deliberate calm beats rushing into the next switch or control input. Teach a brief reset: breathe, prioritize aviate/navigate/communicate, then act. Avoid dumping unrelated life-stress analogies into the moment of the emergency.
Lines of longitude (meridians) cross the Equator at right angles and converge at the poles. Latitude lines are parallel to the Equator. This is basic chart geometry for true course measurement.

Measure true course on a sectional at a meridian near mid-route because meridians converge: the angle between your course and true north changes along the route. Midpoint measurement averages that convergence error.
Wind triangle (typical FAA figure): the line from A to B represents true heading and airspeed (the aircraft vector through the air). Know which leg is TH/AS vs TC/GS vs wind.
Wind triangle: line from C to B represents groundspeed and true course (the path over the ground). That is the course/GS vector you plot on the chart.
Wind triangle: line from C to A represents wind direction and velocity (from wind-dot to air-vector tip, depending on construction). Wind is from → to along that vector.

True course → magnetic heading: apply variation (add west / subtract east — “East is least, West is best”), then apply wind correction (subtract left WCA / add right WCA) to get magnetic heading. Sequence: TC ± var = MC, then ± WCA = MH.
Magnetic course → true course: add easterly variation (and subtract westerly). Going MC→TC is the reverse of TC→MC. Variation depends on location, not on which way the nose is pointed.
True heading → true course: remove the wind correction angle — subtract a right WCA (or add a left WCA). Heading is where the nose points; course is the path over the ground.
Magnetic variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north. It is printed on charts as isogonic lines and changes slowly over years — always use current chart variation.

Answer: 2 only. Bank wording “indication V2” means the sample instrument labeled V (letters T–Z under the gauges)—not a second instrument, and not the TO/FROM flag. Figure note: OBS is set to 180° (18 under the top index on every gauge; 030 at the bottom is only the reciprocal). Read instrument V as a whole: OBS 180 + that needle deflection + FROM. Then find which airplane around the compass rose would see that same picture—only aircraft 2. Airplane heading in the drawing does not change the CDI/TO-FROM; position relative to the station and the OBS setting do. Distractors (6 only; 5 and 8) are other positions that match different lettered indications.
VOR/OMNI figure item: indication U corresponds to aircraft position 6 only. Same method — resolve OBS setting, TO/FROM, and CDI deflection against each numbered position until only one fits.

VOR/OMNI figure item: aircraft 8 would show indication W. Work TO/FROM and left/right sensing from the aircraft’s position relative to the selected course; W is the unique match for that station geometry.

Sectional Figure 44: choose an altitude that stays under the Class B shelves between Northwest (area 2) and McKinney (area 5). Keyed answer is 2,500 feet MSL — read the blue Class B altitude boxes along the route and stay below the floor.

links.label: FAA Chart Users’ Guide — Class B

details.summary: Figure 44 obstruction 10 SM west of McKinney: charted obstruction heights — keyed that the top is 487 MSL or less for that symbol/group. Read the bold MSL number (and AGL in parentheses when shown) on the chart.

Figure 45, McCampbell (area 1): read where controlled airspace begins — keyed as 718 feet MSL for this chart set (often a Class E floor expressed with field elevation context). Always confirm the magenta vignette / chart notes on the figure.

links.label: FAA Chart Users’ Guide — Class E floors

details.summary: Figure 45 near Corpus Christi VORTAC (area 5): controlled airspace begins at 700 feet AGL (magenta vignette Class E transition area). Magenta = 700 AGL floor; soft blue = 1,200 AGL floor.

Figure 45, Bishop to McCampbell at 2,000 MSL: two-way radio is required when entering the Corpus Christi Class C airspace. Outside Class C/D/B, VFR radio may not be required — the trigger is penetrating that Class C.

Figure 45, Cuddihy (area 8): minimum avionics (with owner permission as the stem notes) are two-way radio and a Mode C transponder — because the airport sits in/under Class C / Mode C requirements for that chart area.
Figure 45, NAS Kingsville (area 2): airspace beginning at the surface is Class D (dashed blue airport traffic area). Military fields still use the same Class D depiction when a tower is operating.

Alert areas (Figure 45 area 6): no special clearance or equipment requirement, but pilots should be extremely cautious due to high-volume training. Participation is voluntary awareness — not a clearance regime.
Figure 46, Livermore Class D: the charted ceiling is 2,900 feet MSL (the number in the dashed-blue box). Class D tops are MSL altitudes on the sectional, not “2,500 AGL” by default.
Figure 46 over Hayward (area 3): Class B begins at 1,500 feet MSL per the blue altitude box for that sector. Fly below that floor (or get a clearance) to stay out of Class B.
Figure 46, San Jose Class C: the ceiling is charted at 4,000 feet MSL. Read the magenta Class C altitude stacks on the figure — surface/shelf floors and the top.

On a sectional (Figure 46), the large blue two-digit value like “2a” / MEF in a quadrangle is the Maximum Elevation Figure — highest terrain/obstacle elevation in that grid square, with a safety buffer, expressed in thousands/hundreds of feet MSL.

Figure 46, Gnoss to Rio Vista: use the highest Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) along the route for obstruction clearance planning — keyed 3,200 feet MSL. MEF is the large blue two-digit value in each quadrangle.

Class C outer area (area B on Figure 47) normally has about a 20 NM radius. Procedural ATC services are provided there when participation criteria are met; it is not charted like the Mode C veil of Class B.

A private pilot (ASEL) may act as PIC of an airplane towing a glider if, within the preceding 24 months, that pilot has made at least three flights as PIC of a glider towed by an aircraft (plus the other 61.69 requirements: endorsements, ground/flight training, etc.).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.69 — Glider towing: experience and training

details.summary: The runway/runway hold position sign (red with white runway numbers, often both directions) denotes intersecting runways — hold short of the intersection as directed.

Runway hold position markings on a taxiway (four yellow lines: two solid, two dashed) hold aircraft short of the runway. Solid lines on your side means do not cross without clearance (or CTAF discipline at nontowered fields).
An outbound destination sign identifies direction to takeoff runways (black background with yellow legend/arrow pointing toward the runway complex).
A taxiway location sign (yellow inscription on black background) identifies the taxiway you are on. Direction signs are black on yellow and point toward other taxiways/runways.
Elevators rotate the airplane about its lateral axis (pitch). Teach axes with controls: elevator → lateral, ailerons → longitudinal, rudder → vertical.
Ailerons rotate the airplane about its longitudinal axis (roll). Coordinate with rudder to manage adverse yaw.

Bank answer text looks swapped. True altitude is actual height above mean sea level (calibrated for nonstandard temperature/pressure). Indicated altitude is what you read on the altimeter with local setting.
Absolute altitude is height above the terrain/surface (AGL). Radar altimeters read absolute altitude; you estimate it visually or from chart elevation + true altitude.
Indicated altitude equals true altitude at sea level under standard conditions (when the altimeter setting and atmosphere match the calibration assumptions).
The pitot system supplies impact (ram) pressure to the airspeed indicator. Altimeter and VSI use static pressure only.
Figure 24: at pressure altitude 3,000 ft, raising temperature from 30°F to 50°F increases density altitude about 1,300 feet. Warmer air → higher DA.
Pressure altitude ≈ field elevation corrected for altimeter setting vs 29.92. For 3,563 ft and 29.96, keyed PA is 3,527 ft MSL (slightly below elevation because setting > 29.92).

If equipment has been added beyond original empty weight, allowable useful load decreases (max gross − new empty weight). Always use current empty weight/CG from the latest W&B sheet, not the old POH sample empty weight.

links.label: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

details.summary: A runway exit sign indicates the designation and direction of an exit taxiway from the runway — helps you plan rollout exit without missing the turnoff.
Figure 30 wind component: landing Runway 18 with wind 220° at 30 kt → 40° off the nose. Crosswind ≈ 30 × sin(40°) ≈ 19 knots. Use the wind rose / component chart in the supplement.

High density altitude reduces climb performance (and lengthens takeoff/landing distances). Thin air = less lift and less propeller/engine performance for powered ships; for gliders, true airspeed and energy management change.
Pressure altitude is the altitude indicated when the altimeter’s barometric scale is set to 29.92 in Hg. It is the standard starting point for performance and DA calculations.
If density altitude is beyond chart capability, do not attempt takeoff until conditions allow calculations that show a safe takeoff and climbout. No guesswork past the chart.

Bank answer text looks swapped (airfoil axis wording). Concept for the stem: on older radar summary charts, an echo top like .250 with an underline coded the maximum top height band (tens of thousands of feet). Prefer modern GFA / radar mosaics on aviationweather.gov for current products, and learn the legend of whatever chart the test figure shows.
Public figures (VIP movement) are protected by Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs), often under § 91.141 / FDC NOTAMs. Check NOTAMs before every flight — stadium and VIP TFRs are common.
When changing squawk codes, avoid inadvertent selection of 7500 (hijack), 7600 (lost comm), and 7700 (emergency). Dial carefully through those codes; some panels let you preset then activate.

links.label: AIM 6-4 — Two-way Radio Communications Failure / Emergency codes

details.summary: The ILS critical area boundary sign identifies the edge of the ILS critical area. Do not enter beyond it when ATC protects the ILS (typically low ceilings/visibility) unless cleared.

links.label: AIM 2-3-5 — ILS Critical Area Markings / Signs

details.summary: Bank is mis-topic’d under systems (certificate renewal). Passing a flight instructor practical test in one category/class (e.g., single-engine airplane) renews the instructor certificate with its ratings for the renewal period — you do not need a separate ride in every rating to renew the whole certificate. Confirm current Part 61 renewal paths (FIRC vs practical test).

links.label: 14 CFR § 61.197 — Renewal requirements for flight instructor certification

details.summary: Antidote for antiauthority (“don’t tell me”): “Follow the rules. They are usually right.” Say the antidote, then comply / choose the safer legal option.

Human behavior is cited as a factor in about three out of four accidents — the teaching point behind ADM, CRM, and risk management. Technical skill matters, but judgment and behavior dominate the accident record.

Bank answer text looks swapped (instrument wording). Concept: when turning onto a taxiway from another taxiway, a taxiway directional sign indicates designations/directions of taxiways leading out of the intersection (black legend on yellow) so you select the correct route.
METAR Figure 3 at KBRO: rain begin/end remarks give duration — keyed answer is 25 minutes for that observation. Practice decoding RAB/RAE pairs in the RMK section.

Student pilot certificate applications are submitted to an FSDO, an authorized flight instructor, or a designated pilot examiner (IACRA / in-person process as currently published). Plastic student certificates are issued by the FAA after processing.

Bank answer text looks swapped (instrument wording). Concept for the stem: from Hicks (area 1) northeast toward Northwest (area 2) on Figure 44, read the Class B floors and pick the maximum altitude that remains under the shelf — use the figure’s blue altitude boxes (same skill as bank_634).

links.label: FAA Chart Users’ Guide — Class B

details.summary: Figure 21 among aircraft 1–3: lowest aspect ratio is aircraft 1 (compute span÷chord). Low AR → more induced drag.

A forecast K-index of 35 implies a high likelihood of thunderstorms (commonly taught as about a 60% chance in FAA weather materials). Higher K → more unstable / moist mid-levels → better thunderstorm potential. Cross-check with outlooks, radar, and AIRMETs/SIGMETs.
After scuba diving without a controlled ascent, wait at least 12 hours before flight to cabin altitudes of 8,000 feet or less. Decompression sickness risk rises with altitude after diving.
After scuba diving that required a controlled ascent (decompression stop), wait at least 24 hours before flying to 8,000 feet or less. Longer waits apply for higher cabin altitudes.
K-index +17: expect good afternoon soaring with a chance of showers (moderate instability/moisture). Higher K → better thunderstorm potential; very high K is more storm than soar.
(Figure 8) On a Surface Analysis chart, symbol “12” denotes a squall line. Use the Figure pill; match the legend for fronts, troughs, and squall-line symbology.
Same solo-XC endorsement idea as bank_420: logbook endorsement that preflight planning/preparation was reviewed and the student is prepared to make the flight safely.
If the towplane releases while the glider is in low-tow, the rope can foul the glider’s nose, canopy, or flying surfaces. Prefer high-tow for release; brief rope-on-glider emergencies.

Extending flaps increases wing camber, which increases both lift and drag (for a given AOA/speed regime). That is why flaps allow slower approach speeds but also steeper approaches / more drag for path control.

Trigger temperature is the surface temperature needed for the surface parcel to rise through roughly the first 4,000 feet on a dry adiabatic lapse rate — i.e., when thermals start “triggering” deep convection for soaring.
Yellow demarcation bar marks the boundary between a runway with a displaced threshold and a blast pad, stopway, or taxiway that precedes the runway. Land beyond the displaced threshold markings.
A K-index of 10 indicates little or no thunderstorm potential (stable/dry enough that storms are unlikely). Contrast with K 30+ for high storm chances.
Same key idea as the other stability card: the most desirable stability is positive dynamic stability — disturbances damp out over time and the aircraft returns to equilibrium.

Gliders usually feel ground effect at less than about half the wingspan above the surface. Long-span ships therefore enter ground effect higher than short-span trainers — plan the roundout accordingly to avoid prolonged float.
Same marking purpose as bank_692: the yellow demarcation bar delineates a displaced-threshold runway from the preceding blast pad/stopway/taxiway.

Induced drag is the portion of total drag created by producing lift, and it changes a lot with airspeed (high at low speed). Duplicate of the core induced-drag teaching point — hammer it for the oral.

In a developed spin, load factor is typically low — about 0.5 to 1.5 G — not a high-G spiral. That is why “it doesn’t feel violent” can lull pilots; airspeed and turn rate still matter for recovery and structural limits after recovery.
Lift is the net force perpendicular to the relative wind — same definition card as bank_009. Keep drag parallel to relative wind; do not measure lift off the horizon.

This bank row is OCR-corrupt (broken id/stem/choices). Teaching point usually intended: moist air masses commonly bring poor visibility, stratiform clouds, and stable conditions compared with dry/continental air. Prefer a clean air-mass question from PHAK until this card is repaired in the import.

details.summary: A 100-hour inspection is required under 91.409(b) when the glider is carrying persons for hire (flight instruction for hire or paid sightseeing). An annual inspection is still required in addition to the 100-hour.

Club/demo sightseeing in a glider can avoid Part 119 because 119.1(e)(5) excepts nonstop commercial air tours in an airplane or glider that begin and end at the same airport and stay within 25 SM of the takeoff airport. Part 91.147 / Part 136 sightseeing rules do not apply to gliders, but 91.409(b) 100-hour inspection still applies when carrying persons for hire.

Under 61.129(f)(2), if you already have 200 hours in heavier-than-air aircraft, the commercial glider path requires 20 glider PIC flights; 3 hours dual (or 10 training flights) including 3 practical-test prep flights in the 2 calendar months before the test month; and 5 solo flights covering the 61.127(b)(6) areas of operation.

14 CFR 91.309: towline at least 200 ft; breaking strength 80–200% of glider max certificated operating weight. If the rope is stronger than twice MGW, install a glider-end safety (weak) link rated 80–200% MGW and a stronger towplane-end link (not more than 25% greater than the glider-end link and not more than 2× MGW).

Adding a glider category rating to an existing commercial airplane certificate generally does not require a new commercial knowledge test under 61.63. You still complete the commercial glider practical test using the additional-rating requirements in the PTS/ACS.

Airplane commercial → glider add-on required table: Navigation (VIII) is NONE. You typically also skip I.A Certificates, II.D Flight Deck Management, and III.A/C — but the evaluator may still sample skipped tasks, so prepare them.

Boxing the wake means maneuvering on tow in a rectangular pattern slightly outside the towplane’s wake while staying coordinated and in control (PTS IV.E). The Glider Flying Handbook cautions not to practice it below about 1,000 ft AGL.
PTS three-way exchange: “You have the flight controls” / “I have the flight controls” / “You have the flight controls,” followed by a visual check that the other pilot has the stick.

If both glider and towplane fail to release, the commercial PTS covers it as oral only (IV.G): discuss signals, low-tow on final, and the glider landing first while the towplane stays high enough to clear.

Without an MEL, inoperative equipment is handled under 91.213(d): remove or deactivate the item, placard it, and determine the aircraft is still safe. Required instruments (for example airspeed per the POH) must work — you cannot placard away a required ASI.
Commercial landing standard: touch down in the designated area and stop short of — and within 100 ft of — the designated point without rolling past it (light-to-medium braking).
Minimum sink and speed-to-fly are separate performance speeds. On the commercial test you must know the concepts and hold each selected speed within ±5 knots (PTS Area V).
Simulated off-airport landing on the commercial test is flown at an established airport without using the altimeter. Field-selection knowledge is covered orally.

14 CFR 61.133 lets a commercial pilot act as PIC of a glider carrying persons or property for compensation or hire and otherwise exercise commercial privileges in that category. Airplane commercial privileges do not automatically transfer into a glider — you need the glider rating and operate within glider privileges.

Towline / rope-break is on the commercial glider practical test. FAA-S-8081-23B Area IV Task G (Aerotow — Abnormal Occurrences) includes towline break and related abnormals; the evaluator may simulate the failure.

On the slips task the evaluator picks forward, side, or turning slip. Demonstrate the slip without drag devices, hold track, and for the 2-33 initiate recovery so you are out of the slip by 50 ft remaining (POH guidance).

Commercial stall recognition/recovery: choose an entry altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL. Recover at the first buffet or when control effectiveness decays rapidly — do not wait for a deep stall.
Commercial steep turn: 720° of turn at 45° ±5° bank, airspeed ±5 kt, and rollout on the entry heading ±10°.
A 2-33’s published L/D is about 23:1, but XC planning should use roughly half of that (about 11:1, or ~2 NM per 1,000 ft) so you still make a field with margin for sink and wind.

Under 14 CFR 91.211, the required minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for any time exceeding 30 minutes between cabin pressure altitudes of 12,500 and 14,000 feet MSL (inclusive). Above 14,000 feet MSL, the required crew must use oxygen continuously. Passengers have separate requirements above 15,000 feet.

Supplemental oxygen rules are time-and-altitude based for the required crew; passengers have a higher altitude trigger. Hypoxia sneaks up — use oxygen before you “feel fine.” High density altitude thins air: true airspeed reads higher for the same IAS, and both towplane and glider performance suffer — plan longer rolls and weaker climb.

FOI defines learning as a change in behavior from experience — mere exposure without usable change does not qualify.

Principles map: clear objective/prepared learner → readiness (learner is prepared and has a clear objective); practice toward a goal → exercise; emotional result → effect; first-learned → primacy (what is learned first sticks hardest); vivid/real → intensity; last-practiced → recency (what was practiced most recently is remembered best).
Practice directed toward a goal is exercise. Undirected repetition is not the same principle.
Effect ties learning to the learner’s emotional result — satisfying outcomes stick; threat and frustration work against retention.
“Most often repeated → best remembered” is exercise (use it or lose it), not recency (what was practiced most recently is remembered best) or intensity.
Intensity: vivid, realistic, or striking experiences beat dull substitutes. “Real thing vs substitute” is the intensity clue.

New learning crowding out old learning is interference (a forgetting path).
Emphasizing a strength to offset a perceived weakness is compensation (covering a weakness by stressing a strength elsewhere).
Denial (refusing to accept an obvious truth) refuses to accept an obvious truth about performance or risk — confront gently with facts and standards.
Repression (pushing unpleasant feelings or memories out of awareness) pushes threatening feelings out of awareness — including a hidden fear of flying that quietly blocks learning.

Assessment should mirror the objective: knowledge checks for facts, performance checks for skills, and both when both matter.
Authentic / performance assessment fits real-world and critical-thinking skills better than isolated recall items.
Treat anxiety with clear objectives, honest reassurance, and achievable steps — ridicule and surprise standards make it worse.
Integrated instruction starts outside/inside reference early and keeps both in the habit pattern — do not postpone instruments to “later.”

details.summary: Performance, airspace, and regs knowledge before solo belongs on a pre-solo knowledge test — confirm the book knowledge before release.

For airmen certification under Part 1/61, aircraft category means the broad grouping: airplane, rotorcraft, glider, or lighter-than-air. Do not confuse that with airmen class (e.g., single-engine land) or with aircraft-certification categories such as normal/utility.

For airmen certification, class subdivides a category—examples for airplanes are single-engine land and sea, multiengine land and sea. Gyroplane/helicopter lists are rotorcraft classes; airplane/glider lists are categories, not classes.

When the stem says certification of aircraft (not airmen), category means the design/operating grouping: normal, utility, acrobatic (and similar). Airplane/rotorcraft/glider here is the airmen sense of category—wrong frame for this question.

For aircraft certification, class means the same broad airframe types used as airmen categories: airplane, rotorcraft, glider, balloon. Normal/utility/acrobatic are aircraft categories; transport/restricted are certification categories/special purposes—not “class” here.

Part 1 defines night as the period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight. Sunset-to-sunrise and the “1 hour after/before” windows are different rules (e.g., lighting or passenger-currency night landings)—not this definition.

VA is design maneuvering speed—the maximum speed at which full abrupt control application will not overstress the airframe. VNE is never-exceed; VLO is maximum landing-gear operating speed—different letters, different limits.
VFE is maximum flap extended speed—do not fly faster with flaps down than this placard. VLOF is lift-off; “VFC” is not the standard flap-limit designator on the written.
VLE is maximum landing gear extended speed (gear may remain down). VLO is maximum gear operating speed (while extending/retracting); VFE is flaps—common swap on this item.
VNO is maximum structural cruising speed—the top of the green arc; above it (yellow arc) only in smooth air. It is not VNE (red line) and not merely a vague “normal operating range” label.

VSO is stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (gear/flaps as for landing)—bottom of the white arc. VS is the specified-configuration stall; do not mix in takeoff-safety (V2) wording.

Airworthiness Directives under Part 39 are mandatory regulatory requirements, not advisory or voluntary. Owner/operator compliance is required before further flight unless the AD itself (or an approved AMOC) provides otherwise.

You may operate noncompliant with an AD only when that AD (or an FAA-approved alternative method of compliance) expressly allows continued operation under stated conditions. ADs are not voluntary, and IFR is irrelevant to the exception.

After preventive maintenance, Part 43 recordkeeping requires an entry describing the work plus the approving person’s signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held. Date/name alone, or only an airframe-log “full detail” without certificate data, is incomplete.

§43.7 is the rule that authorizes who may approve preventive maintenance for return to service (including a pilot holding at least a private certificate for that aircraft). §91.403 addresses owner/operator maintenance responsibility; §61.113 is private-pilot privilege/limitation—not the return-to-service authority cite.

A private or commercial pilot may perform and approve listed preventive maintenance for return to service on an aircraft they own or operate. Student and recreational pilots lack that Part 43 privilege.

Part 43 Appendix A preventive maintenance includes simple servicing such as replenishing hydraulic fluid. Structural skin seams or landing-gear brace-strut repairs are maintenance/repair work, not preventive maintenance.
Replenishing hydraulic fluid is classic Appendix A preventive maintenance. Repairing landing-gear brace struts or adding skin seams is structural repair—outside the preventive-maintenance list.

§61.3 requires you to have (or have readily accessible) an appropriate pilot certificate and a current medical when a medical is required for that operation. Flight-review endorsements and currency logbook entries matter for privileges, but they are not the documents that must be in your personal possession under this rule.

You must have a current pilot certificate in personal possession or readily accessible whenever acting as PIC or as a required crewmember—not only with passengers, and not for ground crew-chief duties.

As PIC or required flight crewmember, recreational/private pilots must carry a current medical if required plus an appropriate pilot certificate. A flight-review endorsement belongs in the logbook; it is not stamped on the certificate and is not the §61.3 possession item.

§61.3 requires presentation of a pilot or medical certificate upon request of the Administrator, NTSB, or any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer. Broader “DOT representative” or vague “person of authority” wording is not the regulatory list.

To carry passengers as PIC you need a flight review (or qualifying proficiency check) within the preceding 24 calendar months under §61.56. Do not confuse that interval with 90-day passenger landing currency or with an annual review myth.

§61.57 passenger-carrying recent flight experience is three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days in the same category and class (and type if a type rating is required). Flight review uses 24 calendar months—different clock.
The 90-day passenger landings must be in the same category and class, and in the same type if a type rating is required—not merely make/model, and type is not optional when a type rating applies.

After a permanent mailing-address change, §61.60 allows only 30 days of certificate privileges before you must notify the Airmen Certification Branch. Sixty- and ninety-day figures are common distractors.

§61.69 glider-tow PIC experience requires (among other items) 100 hours PIC in the category, class, and type (if required) of the tow aircraft—not 100 hours of any flight time, and not a 200-hour threshold.

Within the preceding 24 months a tow PIC must have made at least three actual or simulated glider tows while accompanied by a qualified pilot (or meet the other §61.69 currency options). Observer rides or powered-glider flights alone do not satisfy that tow-currency item.

A flight review is valid for 24 calendar months; “calendar month” runs to the last day of the month. A review on August 8 is good through August 31 two years later—not the anniversary date, and not one year later.
§61.56 requires a flight review within the preceding 24 calendar months to act as PIC. There is no FAA annual or semiannual flight-review cycle for recreational/private pilots.
Same calendar-month rule: review completed August 8 expires at the end of August two years later (August 31). Choosing the same calendar day or a one-year end-of-month date are classic traps.

A private pilot glider rating does not require an FAA medical certificate; glider operations are exempt from the usual Part 61 medical carriage rule. You still may not act as crewmember if you know or have reason to know of a medical condition that would make you unable to meet the requirements (§61.53).

Under §61.113 a private pilot may share only a pro rata share of operating expenses limited to fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees—and must not pay less than that share. Being paid for carrying passengers “for business” or refusing any expense share are both wrong.

Same private-pilot expense rule: only a fair pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport costs, or rental fees with passengers. Ninety-day landing currency does not authorize compensation, and “no payment of any kind” overstates the limitation.

§61.113’s charitable-flight exception allows a private pilot to carry passengers who donate for the flight when the donation goes to a charitable organization meeting the rule’s conditions. Passengers simply paying all operating expenses is not that exception.
Unless otherwise designated, a Federal airway extends 4 nautical miles either side of centerline (8 NM total width). Six- and eight-NM “either side” figures are common mix-ups with the total width.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Unless otherwise specified, Federal airways are Class E from 1,200 feet AGL up to and including 17,999 feet MSL. 700-foot AGL floors are transition areas; 18,000 MSL is Class A territory—not the airway top.

Basic VFR in Class D needs at least a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility (§91.155). One-mile visibility is Class G daytime below 1,200 AGL territory; 2,500/3 is not the Class D standard.
§91.3 makes the pilot in command directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft—above FAA, manufacturer, or other parties for that flight’s conduct.
Passenger pre-launch briefing is a PIC duty under the PIC’s operational responsibility (§91.3 / passenger-briefing rules)—not the safety officer’s or ground crew’s regulatory role.

In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, §91.3(b) lets the PIC deviate from Parts 91 (and related FARs) to the extent required to meet that emergency. No prior Administrator approval is needed; a written report is only if requested—not automatic within 24 hours.
After an emergency deviation under §91.3, a written report to the Administrator is required only upon request—not within a fixed 7- or 10-day window.

§91.7 places on the PIC the duty to determine whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight before each flight. Owner/operator maintains airworthiness over time; the mechanic inspects/repairs—different hats from the go/no-go call.

Aircraft operating limitations are in the FAA-approved Airplane/Glider Flight Manual, approved manual material, markings, and placards—or any combination. They are not on the airworthiness certificate and not buried as the primary source in maintenance logbooks.

§91.15 allows dropping objects if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property on the surface. It is not limited to emergencies and does not require prior FAA permission for every drop.
The “bottle-to-throttle” rule in §91.17 is 8 hours since the last alcoholic beverage before acting as a crewmember. Twelve- and twenty-four-hour figures are common safety slogans, not this FAR.

§91.17 generally bars carrying a person who appears intoxicated or under the influence of drugs, except in an emergency or when the person is a medical patient under proper care. “No conditions” and cockpit-access limits are incorrect.

Blood-alcohol limit for crewmembers is 0.04 percent by weight or more (§91.17)—ten times larger than the 0.004 distractor and unrelated to the 0.008 figure. The 8-hour rule is separate from this BAC ceiling.

§91.103’s core preflight duty is to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. Logbook checks and wake-turbulence review may be good practice but are not the specific regulatory phrasing tested here.

For flights not in the vicinity of an airport, §91.103 specifically requires considering an alternate course of action if the flight cannot be completed as planned. That is not the same as formally filing/designating an alternate airport (IFR concept).

For VFR away from the vicinity, §91.103 also specifically requires runway lengths at airports of intended use and takeoff/landing distance data for the aircraft. Light-gun procedures and ELT/nav checks are not that listed preflight item.
Flight crewmembers must keep safety belts and shoulder harnesses fastened during takeoff and landing (§91.105). The rule does not require both for all flight conditions or only in turbulence.

Crew rule split: safety belts required during takeoff, landing, and en route; shoulder harnesses during takeoff and landing (when installed). Swapping which restraint applies en route is the usual trap.

PIC must brief passengers on belt use and notify them to fasten belts during taxi, takeoff, and landing (§91.107). Continuous all-flight fastening for passengers is not the regulatory minimum, and “no obligation” is false.
With stated exceptions, passenger safety belts must be secured during taxi, takeoffs, and landings. All-flight or turbulence-only requirements overstate or mis-time the Part 91 passenger-belt rule.

For this stem, the keyed passenger rule is belts secured during taxi, takeoffs, and landings only—not pilots-only at takeoff/landing, and not every occupant for the entire flight as the tested minimum.
Formation flight is prohibited unless each aircraft’s PIC has made a prior arrangement (§91.111). Populated-area or special-VFR Class D bans are not the formation rule’s core test.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Under 14 CFR 91.113(c), an aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic — including balloons and aircraft on final. Category priority and landing rules do not override distress.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: When two aircraft of the same category converge (not head-on), 91.113(d) gives right-of-way to the aircraft on the right — so the one on the left shall give way. Do not confuse this with head-on (both alter right) or overtaking rules.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Among engine-driven aircraft, an aircraft towing other aircraft has right-of-way over all others (91.113(d)). That puts a tow ahead of a gyroplane or airship on this list — do not apply the balloon–glider–airship–airplane ladder alone here.

Category right-of-way order is balloon, then glider, then airship, then airplane/rotorcraft (91.113(d)). A glider therefore has right-of-way over an airship; the towing/refueling privilege applies only over other engine-driven aircraft, so it does not beat a glider.

On a head-on collision course, 91.113(e) requires each pilot to alter course to the right — category priority (glider vs airplane) does not apply to reciprocal approaches. One-sided “yield left/right” choices are wrong.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: When aircraft are approaching to land, 91.113(g) gives right-of-way to the one at the lower altitude — but that aircraft may not use the rule to cut in front of or overtake another. It is not a converging “aircraft on the right” or least-maneuverable test.

Except for takeoff or landing, 91.119(a) sets a universal floor: operate at an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface if a power unit fails. The 500- and 1,000-foot numeric minima are separate paragraphs for specific surface types.

Over congested areas, 91.119(b) requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius of the aircraft. Common traps swap 500/1,000 feet or shrink the horizontal radius to 1,000 feet.

Over other than congested areas, 91.119(c) is 500 feet AGL — except over open water or sparsely populated areas, where you must stay 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure. Do not apply the congested-area 1,000/2,000 numbers or the anywhere emergency-landing rule alone.

In sparsely populated or open-water operations under 91.119(c), you may not operate closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure (except as needed for takeoff or landing). 700 and 1,000 feet are not the Part 91 distance.

If no altimeter setting is available before flight, 91.121 requires setting the altimeter to the elevation of the departure airport/area. Do not invent pressure altitude, density altitude, or a nearby airport’s MSL elevation as substitutes.

Before takeoff, set the altimeter to the current local altimeter setting if available; otherwise use departure airport elevation (91.121). Density or pressure altitude corrections are performance tools, not the pre-takeoff Kollsman setting rule.

When climbing to a cruising flight level, set 29.92 in Hg at 18,000 feet MSL — that is where Class A / flight-level altimetry begins (91.121). 14,500 and 24,000 are common distractors from other airspace numbers.

Once you accept an ATC clearance, 91.123 forbids deviation unless you get an amended clearance — except in an emergency. “Pilot’s discretion” or a restriction in the clearance is not that statutory exception.

If an emergency caused you to deviate from an ATC clearance, a detailed report is required when requested by ATC (91.123) — not automatically “immediately” or on a fixed 7-day clock. Separate rules cover priority-handling write-ups.

If you deviate from an ATC instruction in an emergency and are given priority, 91.123(d) says file a detailed report within 48 hours to the chief of the appropriate ATC facility — if requested. PIC authority alone does not erase the reporting duty, and it is not a generic report to the Administrator ASAP.

Tower light gun to an aircraft in flight: steady green means cleared to land. Flashing green is return for landing; steady red is give way/continue circling — do not swap in-flight and ground meanings.

Alternating red and green from the tower means exercise extreme caution — both in flight and on the surface. Hold position is flashing red (ground); airport unsafe/do not land is steady red to aircraft on the ground or flashing red in flight depending on context — not the red-green alternate.
On a Sectional, Class D is shown as a blue segmented (dashed) circle. Class B uses solid blue rings; Class C uses solid magenta rings — color and solid vs dashed are the trap.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Airspace at a part-time tower airport is Class D only while the associated control tower is in operation. When the tower closes, the airspace reverts as charted (often E or G) — FSS status and VFR weather alone do not create Class D.

Two-way radio with ATC is required for takeoffs and landings at tower-controlled airports regardless of weather (91.129 / Class D rules). The IFR-only or “only when below VFR” distractors mix radio with basic VFR weather minima.
Establish two-way radio communications with the controlling ATC facility before entering Class C (91.130). Class E and G do not impose that prior-radio entry requirement among these choices.

Class C minimum equipment is two-way radio, a Mode C (encoding) transponder, and ADS-B Out (91.130 / 91.215 / 91.225). Radio-plus-bare-transponder or adding DME is incomplete or wrong for this standard.

Operation in Class B requires at least a Private Pilot Certificate, or a Student Pilot Certificate with the appropriate logbook endorsements (91.131). Neither a Commercial certificate nor an instrument rating is the minimum stated rule.
Same Class B pilot minimum: Private, or student with required endorsements (91.131). A Recreational Pilot Certificate or Private-plus-instrument rating is not the regulatory floor for Class B entry.
For VFR in Class B you need two-way radio, Mode C (encoding altimeter), and ADS-B Out (91.131 / 91.215 / 91.225). A VOR/TACAN receiver is not required for VFR Class B on the current exam answer set.

An operable Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required in Class B and within the 30 NM Mode C veil of the Class B primary airport (91.215 / 91.225). Class D and low Class E alone do not trigger that veil rule.
Class A (generally 18,000 MSL up to FL600) is IFR-only — VFR flight is prohibited. Class B and C allow VFR with the appropriate clearances/communications and equipment.

In controlled airspace below 1,200 feet AGL, basic VFR cloud clearance includes 2,000 feet horizontal (91.155 — the “3-152” set). 1,000 or 1,500 feet horizontal are common mis-memorizations of the vertical numbers.
Day Class G at or below 1,200 feet AGL (here 700 AGL) is 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds (91.155). Do not import controlled-airspace 3-152 or the night Class G numbers.
Federal airways below 10,000 feet MSL are Class E controlled airspace, so VFR flight visibility is 3 miles (91.155). One-mile Class G daylight figures do not apply on an airway.
On an airway below 10,000 MSL, cloud clearance is 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal (91.155 “3-152”). Swapping above/below or saying “clear of clouds” is the usual trap.

In controlled airspace more than 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL, VFR requires 1,000 feet above clouds (with 500 below and 2,000 horizontal). 500 feet is the below-clouds figure, not the above-clouds minimum.

Below 10,000 MSL in controlled airspace above 1,200 AGL, VFR is 3 miles visibility with 500 feet below or 1,000 feet above the clouds (plus 2,000 horizontal). The 5-mile / 1,000-and-1,000 set belongs at or above 10,000 MSL, not Class A.
Outside controlled airspace (Class G), daylight VFR above 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 MSL needs only 1 mile flight visibility (91.155). Three miles is the controlled-airspace value in that band.
At or above 10,000 feet MSL and more than 1,200 feet AGL in controlled airspace, VFR flight visibility jumps to 5 miles (91.155). Three miles is the below-10,000 controlled standard.

Above 10,000 MSL (and more than 1,200 AGL), horizontal cloud clearance for VFR becomes 1 statute mile — not the 2,000-foot figure used below 10,000. Vertical clearances also become 1,000 above and 1,000 below.

At or above 10,000 MSL and more than 1,200 AGL, VFR still requires 1,000 feet above clouds (with 1,000 below and 1 SM horizontal). The change at 10,000 is visibility and horizontal distance, not a different “above clouds” number.

Basic VFR takeoff or landing at an airport in Class D requires ground visibility of at least 3 statute miles at that airport when reported (91.155(c)/(d)); otherwise flight visibility. One-mile figures are SVFR/Class G traps, and the rule cites ground visibility when available — not ceiling alone in this stem.
Basic VFR in Class D is a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility (91.155). Special VFR can go lower with ATC authorization; clear-of-clouds with 2 miles is not the basic Class D standard.

Besides a valid Airworthiness Certificate, 91.203 requires the Registration Certificate and operating limitations (often in the AFM/POH or placards) aboard. Engine/airframe logbooks stay with maintenance records on the ground; they are not the in-flight ARROW documents.

Except in Alaska, lighted position lights must be displayed from sunset to sunrise (91.209). Civil twilight defines “night” for logging/currency and some other rules — do not mix that clock with the position-light window.

Between cabin altitudes above 12,500 through 14,000 MSL, required flight crewmembers must use supplemental oxygen for that portion of the flight exceeding 30 minutes (91.211). Continuous use from the first minute is the above-14,000 crew rule, not this band.

Unless each occupant has supplemental oxygen, you may not operate above a cabin pressure altitude of 15,000 feet MSL (91.211). 12,500 and 14,000 are the crew time/continuous-use thresholds, not the all-occupant ceiling.
Mode C (encoding) transponder is required in Class A, Class B (and the 30 NM veil of the primary airport), and Class C (91.215). Class D and low E/G are not Mode C airspace by default.

An approved chair-type parachute carried for emergency use must have been packed by an appropriately rated rigger within the preceding 180 days (91.307). Do not confuse packing interval with the 60°/30° intentional-maneuver wear rule.

With listed exceptions, each occupant must wear an approved parachute when intentional bank exceeds 60° or intentional pitch exceeds 30° relative to the horizon (91.307). The distractor “bank over 30°” mixes the pitch limit with the bank limit.

Under 91.309, a glider towline must have a breaking strength not less than 80% of the glider’s certificated maximum operating weight: 0.80 × 700 = 560 pounds. Equal to gross weight (700) or a round 1,000 are common wrong products.
Minimum towline strength is 80% of certificated maximum operating weight: 0.80 × 1,040 = 832 pounds (91.309). Using half the weight or the full gross weight skips the 80% rule.

If towline strength exceeds twice the glider’s maximum certificated operating weight, approved safety links are required at both ends (91.309). For a 700-pound glider that threshold is 1,400 pounds — so 1,450 requires links; 850 and 1,040 do not.

When towline breaking strength is more than twice the glider’s max certificated operating weight, install approved safety links at both the glider attachment and the towplane attachment (91.309). A link at only one end does not meet the rule.
Restricted-category civil aircraft may not normally be operated over densely populated areas (91.313). IFR or Class D operations are not the blanket prohibition this question targets.

Unless specifically authorized, experimental-certificate aircraft may not be operated over a densely populated area or in a congested airway (91.319). Class B floor or Class D primary-airport location is not the default ban stated in the rule.

Ensuring the aircraft is maintained in an airworthy condition is primarily the owner or operator’s responsibility (91.403). The PIC decides go/no-go for a flight; the mechanic performs work — neither owns the continuous-maintenance duty alone.

Determine airworthiness by a preflight inspection plus review of the maintenance records (status of inspections, ADs, return-to-service). An owner’s verbal assurance or a CFI logbook endorsement does not substitute for the records check.

The owner or operator must ensure maintenance personnel make the appropriate aircraft record entries showing approval for return to service (91.405). The mechanic does the work and entry, but ensuring those entries exist is the owner/operator’s duty — not the PIC’s alone.

Under §91.417, the owner or operator must ensure required maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration entries are made in the aircraft maintenance records — including approval for return to service. A repair station or mechanic may do the work and sign the entry, but the owner/operator still owns the duty to see that the record exists.

Airworthiness Directives are mandatory under Part 39; §91.403(a) puts compliance on the owner or operator before further flight (unless an AMOC is approved). Mechanics and repair stations may perform and document the work, but they do not replace the owner/operator’s compliance duty.

Return to service after an annual is shown by the required maintenance-record entry (Part 43 / §91.417) — date, description, and signature of the person approving. Registration dates and panel stickers do not satisfy the regulatory record of inspection completion.

After an alteration or repair that substantially affects flight characteristics, §91.407 requires an appropriately rated pilot to flight-test and make a maintenance-record entry before carrying passengers. The limit is passenger carriage — not “any private pilot ops” or only for-hire flights.

§91.407 sets the minimum certificate for that operational flight test at a Private Pilot Certificate (appropriately rated). Commercial or instrument ratings are not required for the test flight itself — the rule is about category/class rating and the passenger-carriage restriction until the entry is made.

An annual inspection is due within the preceding 12 calendar months (§91.409). Completed July 12 this year means it remains valid through the end of July next year — due no later than July 31 next year — not the anniversary day or the first of the month.

Annual inspection status lives in the aircraft maintenance records (§91.417), not on the Airworthiness or Registration Certificate. Those certificates show eligibility/registration; the log entry shows when the last annual was completed and by whom.

A Standard Airworthiness Certificate remains effective only while the aircraft is maintained and operated under the FARs (including inspections, ADs, and required equipment). It is not tied to registration currency alone, and “indefinite unless damaged” skips the continuous airworthiness duty.

Aircraft used for hire (including rental) and for flight instruction need both a current annual and a 100-hour inspection under §91.409. The 100-hour does not replace the annual when both apply — and there is no 50-hour or “biannual” substitute in Part 91.

AD compliance is documented in the aircraft maintenance records. The Airworthiness/Registration Certificates and POH do not serve as the compliance record — look for the method, date, and sign-off in the logs.

49 CFR Part 830 requires the operator to notify the nearest NTSB field office immediately (by the most expeditious means available) when an aircraft accident involving substantial damage occurs — not within 48 hours or 7 days. The written report follows on a separate timeline.

links.label: 49 CFR Part 830 — NTSB Notification and Reporting

details.summary: Among listed Part 830 incidents, flight-control system malfunction or failure requires immediate NTSB notification. A forced landing from engine failure or gear damage from a hard landing alone is not in that immediate-notification list unless it meets the accident definition.

links.label: 49 CFR Part 830 — NTSB Notification and Reporting

details.summary: An in-flight fire is a Part 830 incident requiring immediate NTSB notification. Generator/alternator failure or loss of a VOR receiver is not on that immediate-notification list by itself.

links.label: 49 CFR Part 830 — NTSB Notification and Reporting

details.summary: An overdue aircraft believed to be involved in an accident triggers immediate NTSB notification under Part 830. In-flight radio or electrical-generator failures alone do not.
