details.summary: Angle of attack is the acute angle between the wing chord line and the relative wind. Angle of incidence is fixed in the airframe (chord vs longitudinal axis); dihedral is the upward tilt of the wings — neither is AOA.

By definition, angle of attack is chord line versus relative wind. Climb angle vs horizon is flight-path geometry; longitudinal axis vs chord is angle of incidence — a built-in rigging angle, not AOA.

Frost roughens the wing and spoils the smooth boundary layer, cutting lift and raising takeoff distance/stall risk — even a thin layer. It does not usefully increase camber or lower stall speed; treat frost as a no-go contaminant.

Inherent stability means the airplane tends to return toward equilibrium after a disturbance, so the pilot needs less continuous correcting input. Stability is not the same as being hard to stall or spin-proof.

Longitudinal (pitch) stability is set mainly by where the CG sits relative to the center of lift/pressure — an aft CG shortens the restoring moment arm. Rudder/trim effectiveness and the four-force balance are not the primary longitudinal-stability determinant.

The rudder’s primary job is yaw control about the vertical axis. Ailerons control roll; overbanking tendency is managed with aileron (and sometimes opposite aileron in steep turns), not by assigning the rudder that role.

Flaps increase both lift and drag so you can fly a steeper approach path at a given (or lower) approach speed — they increase the angle of descent without requiring more airspeed. The trap choice reverses “increase/decrease descent.”

One purpose of wing flaps is steeper landing approaches without speeding up — more drag (and lift) lets you aim steeper while holding approach speed. They are not trim devices, and they increase effective camber/area rather than decreasing wing area.

Pitot-static instruments are the airspeed indicator (pitot + static), altimeter (static), and VSI (static). Clogging both pitot and static vents knocks out that trio; gyro instruments (attitude, turn coordinator) are independent of the pitot-static system.
Impact (ram) pressure from the pitot tube feeds only the airspeed indicator. Altimeter and VSI use static pressure alone, so a pitot-only clog leaves them working while ASI fails or freezes.

Static pressure drives the altimeter and VSI and is also the reference side of the ASI — so clogged static vents take out airspeed, altimeter, and vertical speed together. “Airspeed only” or “altimeter only” understates the shared static feed.

Setting the local altimeter setting makes the altimeter read true altitude (approximate height above MSL) when you are on the ground at that field. Absolute altitude is height above the surface; “calibrated altitude” is not the altimeter-setting definition.

On a warmer-than-standard day, pressure surfaces are raised, so for a given indicated altitude you are actually higher — indicated altitude is lower than true altitude. The reverse trap (“indicated higher than true when warm”) flips the rule; remember “from hot to cold, look out below.”
True altitude is the actual vertical distance above mean sea level. Height above the surface is absolute altitude; height above the standard datum plane (29.92) is pressure altitude.
Absolute altitude is height above the terrain/surface beneath you. Indicated altitude is what the altimeter shows; pressure altitude is height above the 29.92 standard datum plane.

Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature — the altitude the airplane “feels” for performance. It is not simply indicated altitude or raw height above the 29.92 datum.

Pressure altitude is what the altimeter indicates when the Kollsman window is set to 29.92 in Hg (standard datum plane). It is not IAS corrected for installation error, and it is not yet corrected for nonstandard temperature (that step yields density altitude).

Indicated altitude equals true altitude when you are at sea level under standard atmosphere conditions (pressure and temperature). Zero mechanical error alone is not enough if pressure/temperature are nonstandard; FL180 on 29.92 is pressure altitude, not a true=indicated guarantee.

Rough rule: 1.00 in Hg ≈ 1,000 feet of indicated altitude. Raising the setting from 29.15 to 29.85 is +0.70 in Hg → about a 700-foot increase in indicated altitude — not 70 feet, and not a density-altitude change.
The pitot system supplies impact (ram) pressure only to the airspeed indicator. Altimeter and VSI are static-system instruments and do not use pitot impact pressure.

For a given weight and configuration, indicated stall speed is essentially constant with altitude because the wing stalls at a critical AOA tied to dynamic pressure. True airspeed at stall rises with altitude; do not equate TAS changes with IAS stall changes.

The red line (red radial) on the ASI is VNE — never-exceed speed. Maneuvering speed (VA) and rough-air / design cruise limits are different markings or unpublished values — do not swap them for the red line.

Indicated stall speed in a given configuration stays essentially the same as altitude increases; the wing still stalls at the same critical AOA for that IAS. True airspeed at stall increases with altitude — that is the common mix-up.
ASI red line = VNE (never-exceed). VA (maneuvering) and rough-air speeds are not the red radial — VA often is not color-coded at all.
Never-exceed speed (VNE) is marked by the red radial line. The lower yellow-arc limit is VNO (max structural cruise); the white-arc top is VFE (max flap-extended) — neither is VNE.

Maneuvering speed (VA) is an important structural limit that is not color-coded on the ASI — you get it from the POH/placard. VNE is the red line and VNO is the green/yellow junction; those are coded. (OCR may scramble the keyed choice — teach VA as the uncoded limit.)

Magnetic compass deviation is error from magnetic fields in the aircraft (electrical gear, metal) distorting the local field — corrected with a compass card. Variation is the true-vs-magnetic north geographic difference; magnet flaws are not the definition of deviation.

Northern Hemisphere turning error (UNOS): from a north heading the compass lags. Entering a right turn from north, the card initially shows a turn toward the west. Acceleration errors appear on east/west headings (ANDS), not as the “turn west from north” case.
From a north heading the compass lags: a left turn (toward west) initially shows a turn toward the east. Acceleration on north is not an ANDS case — acceleration errors show on east/west headings.

Acceleration/deceleration errors (ANDS) appear on east or west headings; on north or south headings the magnetic compass indicates correctly during speed changes. It does not “always swing south” or always show a turn when you accelerate.

Northern Hemisphere: starting a left turn from an east heading (turning toward north) produces an initial indication toward the south because of magnetic dip/lead. Do not confuse that with deceleration on west (ANDS) or a right turn from west.

Magnetic compass indications are reliable only in straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight — turns, climbs, and speed changes introduce dip/acceleration errors. Constant airspeed alone is not enough if you are turning or accelerating.

CG aft of the aft limit reduces longitudinal stability and elevator effectiveness for recovery — stall/spin recovery becomes difficult. Forward-CG symptoms (higher stall speed, longer takeoff) are the opposite trap.

Trust the magnetic compass only in straight-and-level unaccelerated flight; turns and speed changes produce known dip and ANDS errors. (OCR may mash this stem with an aft-CG item — the accurate-compass rule is the intended concept.)

Loading to the most aft CG reduces longitudinal stability at all speeds — the restoring moment arm shrinks. Exam traps offer “less stable only at high” or “only at low”; FAA teaching is less stable throughout the speed range, with stall recovery also degraded.
When OAT is warmer than standard at a given pressure altitude, air is less dense, so density altitude is higher than pressure altitude. Cooler-than-standard does the opposite (DA lower than PA).

In a coordinated turn, the horizontal component of lift provides the centripetal force that changes the flight path — that is what makes the airplane turn. Centrifugal force is the equal-and-opposite inertial reaction felt in the turn, not the aerodynamic cause; vertical lift mainly opposes weight.

A spin requires a stall (critical AOA exceeded) plus yaw — both wings are stalled, with one more deeply stalled. A steep diving spiral can be fast and high-G but is not a spin unless the wings are stalled.

Critical angle of attack for a given wing/configuration is fixed — the wing stalls at that AOA regardless of gross weight. Heavier weight raises stall IAS, but not the stall AOA; CG shift changes stick force/stability more than the wing’s critical AOA itself.

Ground effect is the surface altering airflow under the wing so downwash and wingtip vortices weaken. That cuts induced drag near the ground—do not confuse it with added drag or a wing that suddenly stops flying.

Ground effect becomes strong only within about one wingspan of the surface, and is strongest well below that. Twice a span is usually too high for the classic float; high AOA alone is not the height cue.

Near the surface, reduced induced drag means leftover approach speed turns into a long float after flare. Ground effect does not amplify wingtip vortices for wake, and it does not reduce the elevator needed for a full-stall landing.

Lower induced drag in ground effect can let the aircraft lift off before recommended takeoff speed, then settle or mush when it climbs out of the cushion. It does not make a normal-speed takeoff impossible or force an abrupt landing settle by itself.

Stall still occurs at the critical AOA, but higher load factor (bank, pull-up, gust) demands more lift, so that AOA is reached at a higher indicated airspeed. Spin tendency and “harder to control” are separate issues, not the direct load-factor effect asked here.
Angle of attack is chord line versus relative wind—not pitch attitude or any rotor reference. Pitch can change with no AOA change if the flight path changes the same way.

A glider has no thrust; the forward component of weight (gravity along the flight path) supplies the force that overcomes drag. Lift is mostly perpendicular to the relative wind and is not the “engine” substitute.
Best L/D gives the farthest still-air glide for altitude lost. Minimum sink maximizes time aloft, not distance; minimum control speed is unrelated to cruise glide performance.

A gust changes AOA; the resulting load-factor spike grows with dynamic pressure, so higher airspeed means larger structural and G loads in the same turbulence. Slowing reduces the punch—do not reverse that relationship on the test.

In a slipping right turn, too little right rudder for the bank leaves the yaw string and ball displaced toward the high (outside) wing—into the turn’s outside. Skids show the opposite displacement; match both instruments to the slip side, not mixed slip/skid panels.

Excess right rudder entering a right turn produces a skid: yaw string/ball toward the low (inside) wing. That is opposite a slip, so pick the panel pair that both show skid, not the slip illustrations.
Convert NM to feet (~6,076 ft/NM), then divide by the glide ratio: 8 NM ≈ 48,600 ft ÷ 23 ≈ 2,100 ft lost. Distractors usually come from using 6,000 ft/NM wrong or mixing ratio numerator/denominator.
Distance in feet ≈ altitude lost × L/D, then convert to NM: 2,000 × 30 = 60,000 ft ≈ 10 NM. Do not treat the ratio as a direct “miles per thousand feet” without the feet/NM conversion.
Glide ratio ≈ distance (ft) ÷ altitude lost: 9 NM × ~6,076 ≈ 54,700 ft ÷ 2,000 ≈ 27:1. Rounding to 6,000 ft/NM yields a similar choice; 24:1 and 30:1 are common arithmetic near-misses.
Altitude lost = distance in feet ÷ L/D: 15 NM × ~6,076 ≈ 91,100 ft ÷ 22 ≈ 4,100 ft. Using 5,280 ft/NM or flipping the ratio produces the lower distractors.
Same method: 10 NM × ~6,076 ≈ 60,800 ft ÷ 23 ≈ 2,600 ft of sink. 2,400 usually comes from a flat 6,000 ft/NM shortcut; 4,300 from misplacing the ratio.

Into a headwind, fly faster than still-air best L/D so average groundspeed stays up—exam rule of thumb is best L/D plus about half the estimated headwind. Do not add wind to min sink or subtract from best L/D.

Every weather process rides on heat exchange—unequal heating drives pressure differences and motion, not the other way around as the root cause. Pressure differentials and air movement are results of that energy transfer.

Unequal surface heating creates pressure differences, so altimeter settings vary between stations. Terrain elevation and Coriolis affect wind and local climate, but they are not the primary reason settings differ from place to place.

By definition an inversion means temperature rises with height through that layer. Vertical-development clouds and clear air below with haze above describe possible weather effects, not the inversion itself.

The common surface inversion forms when the ground radiates heat away on a clear, calm night and cools the air next to it. Frontal undercutting or rapid mountain lift are other inversion mechanisms, not the most frequent ground-based type.

Under a low-level inversion with high humidity, expect stable, smooth air trapping fog, haze, and low stratus—poor visibility, little turbulence. Showery convective weather belongs to unstable air, not that trapped layer.
ISA sea level is 15 °C and 29.92 in Hg (about 1013.2 mb). Distractors mix °F with millibars or put 59 °C where 59 °F belongs.
Rule of thumb: 1.00 in Hg ≈ 1,000 ft, so 0.15 in lower Kollsman (30.11→29.96) drops the indicated altitude about 150 ft. Lowering the setting always lowers the reading; it does not raise it.

Raising the altimeter setting 0.15 in Hg (e.g., 29.96→30.11) raises indicated altitude about 150 ft—same 1 in ≈ 1,000 ft scale. The setting change itself is not an altitude answer; watch for the “indicate .15" Hg higher” trap.

Pressure altitude equals true altitude only when the entire column matches the standard atmosphere. Setting 29.92 alone makes indicated equal pressure altitude; that does not guarantee pressure altitude equals true height AGL/MSL.
Density altitude equals pressure altitude when temperature is standard for that pressure altitude. Sea-level 0 °F or “no installation error” does not make them the same.
Flying from low toward high pressure without resetting, the altimeter lags with the old low setting and reads lower than you really are. Opposite of “high to low, look out below.”
In colder-than-standard air the column is denser, so true altitude is lower than indicated—same “cold = look out below” hazard as flying toward low pressure. Warm air does the opposite.
Warmer-than-standard air expands the pressure levels, so you are higher than the altimeter shows (indicated lower than true). Cold air and low pressure are the traps that reverse the relationship.

High pressure into lower pressure without updating the setting: the altimeter keeps the old high setting and indicates higher than actual—true altitude is below what you read (“high to low, look out below”).
Higher ambient temperature thins the air and raises density altitude. Higher pressure or lower humidity densifies the air and lowers DA—those choices reverse the effect.

Dewpoint is the temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure, to reach saturation. Dew does not always form at that temperature, and it is not defined as condensation equaling evaporation.

Same concept as the standard dewpoint definition: cool the parcel to saturation temperature—that is dewpoint. “Dew always forms” at that mark is a common wrong wording; condensation needs a surface and other conditions too.
How much water vapor air can hold is set by air temperature—warmer air has higher capacity. Dewpoint tells how much vapor is already present; stability does not set holding capacity.

Visible cloud, fog, or dew requires condensation (or deposition) of water vapor. Merely having vapor, or even 100% RH without condensation onto nuclei/surfaces, is not enough for those products to “always” form.

Moisture enters unsaturated air by evaporation (liquid→vapor) and sublimation (ice→vapor). Heating/condensation and supersaturation are not the adding processes—condensation removes vapor from the air.

Frost forms by deposition when the collecting surface is at or below the dewpoint and that dewpoint is below freezing—vapor goes straight to ice. Freezing rain/drizzle on a cold surface is a different icing process.

Stability is judged by comparing the actual environmental lapse rate to adiabatic rates—how fast temperature falls with height. Surface temperature or pressure alone does not measure that vertical profile.
Warming an air mass from below steepens the lapse rate and decreases stability (more convective). Cooling from below or drying the air tends to stabilize it.
Stable air favors layered stratiform clouds, often with restricted visibility. Cumulus and unlimited visibility point toward unstable or well-mixed conditions instead.
Moist stable air forced upslope cools and forms layered stratus, not convective showers. Thunderstorms and convective turbulence need unstable air.
Lifted unstable air keeps rising, building cumuliform clouds with strong vertical development and turbulence. Stratus with little build-up is the stable-air signature.
A temperature inversion is a very stable layer—rising parcels cool into warmer air above and stop. It is not an unstable layer, and chinooks are a separate mountain-wind phenomenon.

Convective cloud-base rule of thumb: (temp − dewpoint °F) ÷ 4.4 × 1,000 ≈ height AGL. Here 70−48=22 → ~5,000 AGL; add the 1,000 ft field elevation to get ~6,000 MSL. Skipping the MSL add yields a wrong AGL-looking choice.
Same spread method: 82−38=44 °F ÷ 4.4 ≈ 10 → about 10,000 ft AGL. Using ÷4.0 or ÷5.0 pushes answers to 9,000 or 11,000.
Moist unstable air yields cumuliform clouds and showery precipitation. Poor visibility with smooth air, or stratiform showers, describe stable or mixed signatures instead.
Unstable air mixes well: expect turbulence with generally good surface visibility outside of showers. Pairing turbulence with poor visibility or nimbostratus mixes unstable and stable cues.
Stable air resists vertical motion, so flight is typically smooth. Showery precip and turbulence are unstable-air trademarks.
“Nimbus” (or nimbo-) means a rain-bearing cloud—nimbostratus or cumulonimbus. Vertical development is “congestus/towering,” not what the suffix itself denotes.
Cloud families are grouped by height range (low, middle, high, and clouds with vertical development). Shape and composition help naming inside a family, but height is the family divider.
Stationary almond/lens clouds in mountain-wave flow are lenticulars—they can sit still while winds inside are very strong. Funnel clouds and inactive frontal decks look and behave differently.
Standing lenticular clouds mark mountain-wave crests and warn of strong wave lift/rotor nearby. Roll clouds mark the rotor; mammatus hang under thunderstorm anvils—different signals.
Cumulonimbus holds the strongest turbulence (and thunderstorm hazards). Towering cumulus is building toward that stage; nimbostratus is rainy but comparatively smooth layered cloud.
Towering cumulus signals active convection and convective turbulence even before a full CB. Cirrus and nimbostratus do not mark that bumpiness.
The boundary between two air masses is a front (OCR often mangling the word). Frontogenesis is formation of a front; frontolysis is its dissipation—processes, not the boundary name.

Cumulonimbus is the thunderstorm cloud and produces the most severe turbulence of any cloud type. Towering cumulus (OCR often reads “lowering”) already means strong convection, but CB is the “greatest turbulence” pick—not rain-bearing nimbostratus.

Across a front the wind almost always shifts direction—the discontinuity pilots notice most easily. Cloud cover or humidity may change too, but wind direction is the reliable frontal signature on the exam.

Steady, widespread precip ahead of a front means layered stratiform cloud and usually little turbulence. Don’t pair “steady rain” with cumuliform/convective clouds—those give showery rain and bumpier air.

Mountain-wave turbulence needs strong winds roughly perpendicular to a ridge plus stable air so the flow oscillates instead of mixing. Unstable air or flow down a valley/parallel to the ridge is the wrong setup.

Wind shear is simply a change in wind speed or direction over a short distance—it can occur at any altitude and in any direction. The trap is treating it as only a low-level or only a high-altitude problem.

Expect hazardous shear near low-level inversions, frontal zones, and clear-air turbulence. Lenticulars flag mountain wave, and post-frontal stratocumulus flag mixing—not the classic “where shear bites” triad.
Under a surface-based temperature inversion, a wind-shear zone is expected when wind at about 2,000–4,000 feet AGL is at least 25 knots. Memorize 25—not the softer 10 or 15 knot distractors.

Structural icing in flight requires visible moisture (cloud, rain, drizzle) plus subfreezing airframe temperatures. A tight temperature–dewpoint spread or stratiform cloud alone is not enough without that moisture.

Frost roughens the wing and disrupts smooth airflow, cutting lift and raising stall speed—even a thin coat matters. It does not “reshape for more lift” or improve control feel; treat frost as a no-go until removed.

Cumulonimbus needs lifting plus unstable, moist air so parcels keep rising into deep convection. Extra condensation nuclei or “either stable or unstable” miss the instability-and-moisture requirement.
In the cumulus (building) stage the cell is almost all continuous updraft—growth without significant precipitation yet. Roll cloud and frequent lightning belong to later mature/outflow stages.

Precipitation beginning to fall marks the start of the mature stage—downdrafts join the updraft. Anvil tops and peak growth rate are related signs, but rain reaching the surface is the textbook trigger.
Thunderstorms need three ingredients: high humidity (moisture), a lifting force, and unstable air. High temperature or “extensive cloud cover” alone does not replace instability or lift.
The dissipating stage is dominated by downdrafts as the updraft collapses. Cumulus is mostly updraft; mature has both up and down—don’t call mature “downdraft-only.”

Thunderstorms are most intense in the mature stage, when updrafts and downdrafts coexist and precip, gust fronts, and turbulence peak. “Downdraft stage” is not an FAA life-cycle name—dissipating is downdraft-heavy but weaker.

Squall-line thunderstorms generally pose the most intense hazard—a solid or broken line of severe cells, often ahead of a cold front. Steady-state or warm-front storms can be bad, but the squall line is the exam “worst” pick.
A nonfrontal, narrow band of active thunderstorms often developing ahead of a cold front is a squall line. Don’t confuse it with a dry line (moisture boundary) or a vague “prefrontal system” label.

Near airport thunderstorms, the approach hazard to expect is wind-shear turbulence from gust fronts and outflow—even if the cell isn’t overhead. Steady rain is discomfort, not the primary convective approach threat.

Radiation fog favors warm, moist air over low flatland on clear, calm nights when the ground cools the air to saturation. Steam fog (cold air over warm water) and tropical air over cold water are different fog recipes.

A small, shrinking temperature–dewpoint spread means the air is nearly saturated—fog or low clouds are the likely product, especially near 62°F. That pattern is not a thunderstorm or freezing-precip recipe by itself.

Advection fog forms when a moist air mass moves over a colder surface—classic winter inland flow from the cool coastal waters. Upslope/windward mountain moist air and cold air blowing out to sea are different fog types.
Advection fog and upslope fog both need wind to move moist air over a colder surface or up a slope. Radiation/ice fog prefer calm or light wind; don’t group them with the wind-dependent pair.
Thermals develop from solar heating of the surface that unevenly warms the air above it. Inversions suppress convection; static electricity is unrelated to thermal formation.

Near thunderstorms, wind shear and turbulence are the primary soaring hazard—sudden airspeed and attitude changes can exceed structural or control margins. Lightning and static are real but secondary on this question.

Sea-breeze circulation starts because land heats faster than water: cool, dense marine air moves inland under the rising warmer land air. Water does not heat/cool faster than land—that distractor reverses the physics.
A sea-breeze front is usually strongest and most soarable in the afternoon after land–water temperature contrast peaks. Early morning is typically too weak for a useful sea-breeze convergence.
Lightning is the phenomenon always associated with a thunderstorm by definition—electrical discharge. Heavy rain and hail are common but not guaranteed in every cell.

Older test banks use TWEBs for continuous route-oriented transcribed forecasts and winds. Terminal forecasts (TAFs) are airport-specific; area forecasts cover regions, not a tailored route briefing product.
TWEBs were monitored on selected VOR and NDB frequencies, not ATIS or airport advisory freqs. ATIS is local terminal info; don’t mix the two products.

Tell the briefer you intend VFR-only (among other flight details) so the briefing is scoped to VFR hazards and minima. Certificate possession or a formation commander’s address is not the required opener.

A complete preflight weather picture starts with a standard briefing—adverse conditions, synopsis, current/forecast weather, winds, NOTAMs. Abbreviated is an update; “general” is not an FAA briefing type.
If you have no prior weather and leave within the hour, request a standard briefing. Outlook is for long-range planning; abbreviated assumes you already have mass-disseminated or prior data.
Use an abbreviated briefing to fill gaps in mass-disseminated weather (DUATS/internet/TV, etc.). There is no “supplemental” briefing type; outlook is for flights 6+ hours out.
To update a previous briefing, ask for an abbreviated briefing focused on what changed. Don’t restart with a full standard unless you need the whole package again; outlook is for distant departures.

When the departure is 6 or more hours away, the product is an outlook briefing—limited to expected conditions in that time window. “Forecast” or “prognostic” briefing are not official FSS briefing names.
Weather for “tomorrow morning” is far enough out that you request an outlook briefing first. Switch to standard closer to departure when full current data is available.
Ceiling is the AGL height of the lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility into an obscuration. Scattered layers and “thin” clouds do not make a ceiling—don’t count them as one.

Scattered cumulus in a soaring briefing imply active thermals at least up through those lower cloud tops. Thermals do not all stop at cloud base, and high cirrus at 25,000 feet is not your thermal ceiling.

In the figure briefing, thermals are expected by about 1500Z (midmorning) when scattered clouds start forming—visible proof convection has begun. Clear early sky or afternoon wind increase alone is not the thermal-onset cue here.

Continuous transcribed route weather with winds aloft came from TWEB on NDB or VOR. ATIS is airport-terminal only; a “regularly scheduled” VOR weather broadcast is not the same continuous TWEB product.

FAA Advisory Circulars are obtained by downloading from FAA online sources (some free, some for purchase). You do not subscribe via the Federal Register or pick them up as a walk-in from the local FSDO.

details.summary: Beyond a standard briefing, soarers should ask for upper-air soundings to compute thermal index and expected thermal tops. Dry/moist adiabatic rates help cloud-base estimates but are not the “extra soaring ask” keyed here.
Early in the call, give the intended route and destination so the briefer can pull the right area, forecasts, and NOTAMs. Radio frequencies or a home address are not the initial briefing identifiers.
Open by identifying yourself as a pilot so the facility knows to give an aviation weather briefing. Occupant count or total flight time is not part of the initial ID to FSS.
State aircraft identification or the pilot’s name so the briefing can be logged and tailored. True airspeed and fuel on board are flight-plan items, not the weather-call identity fields.
On the sectional, read latitude from the left/right ticks and longitude from the top/bottom—Currituck County sits near 36°24'N, 76°01'W. Watch for 36°48' look-alikes one tick too far north.

details.summary: Between 1,200 AGL and 10,000 MSL in Class E (over Cooperstown), day VFR is 3 SM visibility with 1,000/500/2,000 cloud clearance. Below 1,200 AGL Class G day mins (1 SM, clear of clouds) do not apply at that altitude band.

Magenta vignette means Class E starts at 700 feet AGL, so below that floor you are still in Class G. Day Class G at or below 1,200 AGL is 1 SM visibility and clear of clouds—not the 3-152 or Class B “3 and clear” values that trap people once they see a town or airport nearby.

details.summary: Fort Worth Meacham’s blue dashed ring is Class D with the ceiling printed in the airport data block—3,200 feet MSL. Nearby Class B shelves and Class C depictions are different symbols; do not borrow their tops for Meacham’s surface area.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Class C shelves are charted as altitude pairs in hundreds of feet MSL (e.g., 13 over a higher top means a 1,300 MSL floor). The outer-circle shelf floor is MSL, not AGL—converting to AGL is the usual trap.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Unless otherwise designated, a Federal airway is Class E from 1,200 feet AGL up to—but not including—18,000 MSL (so 17,999 MSL). Traps swap AGL/MSL or invent 700-foot or high-altitude airway floors.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Sectional CAUTION notes state the hazard and the top altitude in MSL—here an unmarked balloon on cable to 3,008 MSL. Swapping MSL for AGL, or inventing hangars from similar numbers, misses the printed note.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: A flag symbol on a VFR sectional is a visual checkpoint for position reports on initial callup to Approach—not a compulsory IFR reporting point. Use it to identify yourself to Norfolk Approach, not as a mandatory radio fix.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Field elevation is the first (top) number in the airport data block beside the airport symbol—for Chesapeake Regional that is 19 feet. Longer numbers nearby are usually longest-runway length or other data, not elevation.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Sectional contour tints band terrain by MSL range; light tan between Minot and Audubon Lake matches the 2,000–2,500 foot band. Do not stretch the band to the next contour interval or treat it as “sea level to ….”

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Flag symbols at airports outside Savannah mark VFR visual checkpoints for the initial call to Approach before entering Class C—not Class C boundaries and not special traffic-pattern airports.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Lighted obstacles show bold MSL height with AGL in parentheses; pick the bold MSL figure (1,548) for “height of the obstacle.” Choosing the AGL value or rounding to a nearby even thousand is the usual miss.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Group obstruction symbols also list the top in bold MSL—here 432 feet MSL near the Savannah 330° radial. Do not substitute a nearby AGL figure or a different obstacle’s elevation.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Read the obstacle’s MSL top from the chart, then add the required 500-foot vertical clearance to get the minimum overflight altitude (1,273 MSL). Adding 500 to AGL, field elevation, or the wrong obstacle yields the distractors.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Same method as other clearance questions: charted obstacle MSL + 500 feet = minimum altitude to clear by 500 (1,403 MSL at Winnsboro). Using AGL-only or airport elevation alone understates the MSL target.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Control tower frequency is the CT value printed in the airport data block (Addison 126.0). 122.95 is typically UNICOM and other nearby frequencies belong to different facilities—match the CT label, not the first number you see.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Nav-aid symbols distinguish VOR, VOR/DME, and VORTAC by the DME/TACAN cue on the compass rose. DFW’s charted facility is VOR/DME—not a plain VOR and not a VORTAC with TACAN channels.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Under normal daytime heating, expect the strongest thermals over surfaces that warm fastest—dark/built-up or dry ground—rather than cool water, swamp, or heavy vegetation. Pick the charted area with that heat-source character (area 2 on this figure).

Final-glide planning applies the recommended safety factor (commonly half the published L/D) to the charted distance, then adds arrival height (1,000 AGL) and destination elevation to get go-ahead MSL. Using full 22:1 without the safety factor produces the lower distractors.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: For that flight’s preflight go/no-go, 91.3 puts the determination that the aircraft is safe on the PIC. Owner/operator maintains airworthiness over time, and the mechanic signed past work—neither replaces the PIC’s preflight judgment today.

First flight of the day means a thorough, systematic preflight using the manufacturer’s checklist—not a casual fuel/oil glance or an improvised PIC sequence. Habit and completeness beat speed on the first launch.

Keeping the aircraft airworthy day-to-day is primarily the owner/operator’s duty (91.403). PIC still decides whether this flight is safe, but ongoing maintenance responsibility is not the mechanic’s alone or the PIC’s maintenance hat.

Advisory Circulars are obtained from the FAA website (home page links to ACs)—not by walking into a district office or by Federal Register subscription alone. ACs are guidance numbered by subject series.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Before each maneuver, clear the area visually for traffic—see-and-avoid comes first. Instrument cross-checks and CTAF calls help, but they do not replace a full visual scan before you commit to the maneuver.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: To hold altitude, upward air must at least match the glider’s current sink rate—there is no fixed “2 fps” minimum. Matching adjacent sink elsewhere does not define the lift you need in the thermal.

Rock heats faster than vegetation, and the sun-facing slope gets the strongest insolation—so the best thermals form on the sunny side of the knoll. Downwind or “exactly over center” ignores where the surface actually warms first.

Converging dust or smoke streamers mark rising/inflow air and are a classic ground clue for thermals. Random expanding circles or a straight downwind track are poor search tactics compared with visible convergence.

Enter a dust devil at or above about 500 feet and work the outer edge circling opposite the vortex rotation so you stay in the rising ring. Circling with the rotation, or entering low into the core, is the hazardous distractor set.

The eye of a dust-devil vortex is turbulent and often weak or descending—avoid it and stay in the rising outer dust. The clear outer edge can still have usable lift; matching rotation direction is not the safety rule.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Active thermals under building Cu often show a smooth cumulus with a concave (domed-up) base where lift is concentrated. Fragmented Cu or a generic “scattered–broken Cu” sky is a weaker or less specific cue.

Bubble thermals from intermittent heating are often marked by soaring birds in those patches—follow the birds. Wet post-shower ground and inversion tops are usually poor thermal sources, not bubble markers.

For cross-country, organized thermal streets give repeatable climb lines between clouds or blue streets—prefer them over warm-front lift or mountain-wave systems for classic thermal XC. Wave and fronts are different energy systems with different risks.

Ridge/slope lift forms on the upwind face of hills or ridges when moderate wind is forced upward. Mountain waves form downwind; strong wind over isolated peaks is often turbulent deflection, not reliable slope lift.
A rotating beacon on in daylight at a towered (Class D) field signals that weather is below basic VFR minimums. It is not an obstruction warning and does not by itself mean the tower is closed.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: A runway painted with a large “X” (or shown that way on the airport diagram) is closed—do not use it. That marking is not a heliport or stabilized overrun symbol.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Runway numbers are magnetic orientation to the nearest 10°, so 9 and 27 mean about 090° and 270° magnetic—not true. Do not read them as 009/027 or as true headings.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Standard Class C over the primary airport normally tops at about 4,000 feet AGL. 1,200 and 3,000 AGL are dimensions from other airspace types—do not reuse them for Class C’s upper limit.
Class C’s outer area normally extends about 20 NM from the primary airport—beyond the charted 5/10 NM Mode C rings. 5 and 15 NM are inner/shelf radii people confuse with the outer area.

In Class C you must operate in compliance with ATC clearances and instructions—VFR is allowed; IFR is not required. Mode C/ADS-B is a separate equipment rule often offered as a distractor for this “must be in …” wording.

Departing a satellite airport inside Class C, establish contact with ATC as soon as practicable after takeoff—you need not file a flight plan solely for that, nor is “monitor until clear” enough by itself.

Transit of a restricted area requires authorization from the controlling agency—not merely being on an airway with a generic ATC clearance, and not a hard “never.” Check status and get the using/controlling agency’s OK.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: VFR pilots may enter an MOA without a clearance, but must exercise extreme caution when military activity is hot. Clearance-before-entry and “airways only” rules apply to other special-use types, not MOAs.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Alert areas warn of high training activity, but collision avoidance still rests with all pilots—there is no controlling agency or ATC that assumes see-and-avoid for you.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Class D lateral limits are sized for the instrument procedures served by that airport—not a fixed 5 SM circle or a count of satellite airports. Chart the actual dashed boundary rather than assuming a textbook radius.
Inside the primary airport’s Class D, even a non-tower satellite requires two-way radio with the primary tower—not the satellite UNICOM or FSS. Talk to the facility that owns the surface Class D.
Before entering an Airport Advisory Area, contact the local FSS for airport and traffic advisories. ATIS/approach are the wrong first call for that advisory function.

Before entering Class C, establish two-way communications with Approach on the charted frequency—Approach owns the shelf/outer area. Calling the tower first for “permission,” or FSS for advisories, is the wrong initial action.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Read the segmented circle’s landing-direction indicator and L-shaped pattern indicators together: they select both runway and left vs right traffic. Here that combination is right traffic for Runway 18—not left 18 or a crosswind runway the sock does not favor.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: The tetrahedron/landing tee points into the wind for the favored runway; if that runway is 18 and the wind is angled, expect a right crosswind component. Landing 22 “straight into wind” ignores the preferred runway the indicator selects; 36 would be downwind.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Segmented-circle L-bars show pattern direction for each runway end: arms on the left mean left traffic, on the right mean right traffic. For this figure that is left traffic on 36 and right traffic on 18—swap those and you have the common reverse-read trap.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: When both pattern directions bend the same way, traffic is kept off one quadrant—here the arrangement keeps flights away from the southeast side. Match which side has no downwind/base path rather than guessing “south” or “north.”

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Combine runway heading with wind-sock direction: Runway 26 with wind from the right-forward quadrant is a right-quartering headwind. Left-quartering or right-quartering tailwind means you mirrored the sock or the runway reciprocal.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Use the wind cone for which runway is into the wind, then the L-bar for left vs right traffic on that runway—here left traffic on Runway 36. Picking a crosswind runway or the reciprocal pattern direction is the usual error.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Wingtip vortices exist only when the wing is producing lift—not merely because the airplane is fast or heavy. Heavy/slow/clean worsen strength, but generation itself requires lift.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Wake is strongest behind a heavy, clean, slow airplane—maximum weight, flaps/gear up, high angle of attack. “Dirty and fast” or “light” configurations produce weaker vortices.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Wingtip vortices sink below the generating aircraft’s flight path—so the hazard is underneath and behind, not rising into the pattern or up into a crossing runway’s path.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Wingtip vortices sink and drift with the wind after rolling up behind a generating aircraft, so the hazard is below and behind—not rising into the pattern. Stay above the heavy’s path and avoid the area under its flightpath on takeoff or landing.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: A light quartering tailwind holds vortices over the runway and drifts them into the touchdown zone longest—worst case for landing wake. Strong headwinds or quartering headwinds move the wake clear faster; do not treat those as the maximum-caution case.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Maximum caution on landing wake is a light quartering tailwind—it keeps vortices on and along the runway. Do not confuse that with a quartering headwind, which usually clears the runway sooner.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Landing behind a large aircraft: stay at or above its final-approach path, note the touchdown point, and land beyond it so you stay out of sinking vortices. Flying below and touching down short is the classic trap into the wake.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Over national wildlife refuges, the requested minimum overflight altitude is 2,000 feet AGL—not 1,000 or 3,000. Treat the chart note as an operational request even when it is not a hard FAR floor.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: In haze, reduced contrast makes traffic and terrain look farther away than they are, so you close on them faster than expected. That distance illusion—not “eyes focused at infinity”—is the exam trap.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Daylight traffic scan is short, regularly spaced eye stops across roughly 10° sectors so each patch gets focused vision. Continuous windshield sweeping or only watching 3/9/12 o’clock misses most of the sky.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Left/right scan in cruise means systematically focusing on successive sky segments for short intervals, then moving on. Smooth continuous sweeps and relying mainly on peripheral motion detection both leave gaps.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: A collision course shows little or no apparent relative motion against the windshield—the target stays fixed while growing slowly. Rapid apparent movement or “both noses aimed at one point” is not the reliable cue.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: An ATC clearance authorizes you to proceed under the conditions stated—it is not a guarantee of separation from all traffic and does not give priority over everyone. You still own see-and-avoid and compliance with the clearance limits.

Hypoxia means oxygen deficiency in the body—distinguish it from hyperventilation (excess ventilation) and decompression sickness (gas bubbles in joints/tissues). Altitude and time drive the risk; symptoms can be subtle.

Rapid or extra-deep breathing on oxygen dumps CO₂ and produces hyperventilation—not sinus or ear block. Match breathing rate to need; over-breathing the mask is a common setup for tingling and lightheadedness.

Emotional tension, anxiety, or fear commonly drive the rapid breathing that causes hyperventilation. Alcohol and slow under-breathing are different problems; do not mix those distractors with the CO₂-loss mechanism.
Restore CO₂ by slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a bag, or talking aloud—do not speed up ventilation. Staring harder at instruments does not fix the chemistry; increasing rate worsens it.

In poor visual conditions, trust the flight instruments over seat-of-the-pants cues—inner-ear and muscle sensations lie. Rapid outside/panel eye shifts or “leaning against” the turn deepen spatial disorientation.

Reduce spatial-disorientation risk by believing the instruments rather than vestibular/muscle feel when outside references are poor. Fast outside–panel eye switching is a distractor that can make the problem worse.

Temporary confusion from conflicting sensory inputs to the brain is spatial disorientation—not hyperventilation or hypoxia. Those other terms are separate aeromedical states with different causes and fixes.

You are more prone to spatial disorientation when you use body/inner-ear signals to judge attitude instead of instruments. Ignoring those sensations and cross-checking instruments is protective, not the hazard.

Once disoriented in restricted visibility, recover by relying on aircraft instrument indications and flying the attitude they show. Concentrating on yaw/pitch/roll “feel” or treating it like hyperventilation keeps you in the sensory trap.
Advisory Circular subject series 60 covers Airmen topics; 70 is Airspace and 90 is Air Traffic/General Operations. Match the series number to the subject family, not the individual AC title alone.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: ACs on Air Traffic Control and General Operations use subject number 90 (e.g., wake and collision-avoidance guidance). Do not pick 60 (Airmen) or 70 (Airspace) for that family.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Winch porpoising is cured by relaxing back-pressure and shallowing the climb angle so the cycle damps out. Pulling in phase with the oscillation or calling for more winch speed deepens the pitch porpoise.

Solo below placarded minimum pilot weight requires enough seat ballast to reach that minimum—here 115 lb needs about 20 lb of ballast (to 135+, meeting 135/138 min). Do not average toward mid-weight or dump ballast in the rear seat as a substitute.

When solo weight is under the placarded minimum, add only the ballast needed to reach that minimum—125 lb against a 134/135 lb floor means about 10 lb in the seat. Averaging to 170 lb or loading the rear seat alone is the common overshoot trap.

Weight-and-balance CG = total moment ÷ total weight; use the figure’s arm stations for empty glider, forward pilot, and aft passenger, then compare to the published CG limits. Mis-adding moments or swapping seat arms yields the out-of-limits forward distractors.

Adding mass forward of the current CG (station 43.8 vs a ~82-inch CG) shifts CG forward; recompute new moment and weight, then check limits. Direction matters—equipment ahead of CG cannot shift CG aft.

Equal heavy pilot and passenger weights still need full moment math against Figure 54 arms; check both CG band and max gross. A matching CG number that exceeds max weight is a different fail—read both conditions on the choice.

On the polar/performance figure, sink distance for 1 SM at a stated speed is altitude lost over that mile—read the chart at 53 MPH, not nearby min-sink or best-glide speeds. Mixing those speeds produces the 144/211 ft distractors.

Find the airspeed on the polar where sink rate equals the asked value (here 5 ft/sec in still air)—interpolate the figure carefully between nearby marks. Do not grab min-sink or best L/D unless that is what the scale shows at that sink rate.

Minimum-sink speed maximizes time aloft, not distance; read feet of descent per statute mile at that min-sink point on Figure 55. Best L/D altitude loss per mile is a different number—common swap with the 170/132 choices.
Most distance for a given altitude loss is best L/D speed—on Figure 55 that is the speed with the flattest glide (here 53 MPH), not min sink (slower) or a high-speed penetration point.

Lift/drag at a given speed equals horizontal distance ÷ altitude lost over that distance from the polar (or the charted L/D). At 68 MPH read the matching ratio; do not use the peak L/D unless the speed is best glide.

On the standard aerotow signal sheet (Figure 56), illustration 2 is “hold position”—wingwalker/arms posture that freezes the launch. Do not confuse it with ready-to-tow or release-towline signals nearby on the same plate.

Figure 56 illustration 3 is the ground signal to release the towline. Stop-operations and take-up-slack use different postures—match the arms/wingwalker pose to the legend, not the nearest similar figure.

Stop-operation on the tow signal chart is illustration 7—learn that number separately from hold (2) and release towline (3). Mixing launch-line signals with airborne sailplane signals is a frequent miss.
Sailplane-to-towplane “turn right” is illustration 5 on Figure 56—distinct from left-turn and other in-flight bank/rudder signals. Confirm which aircraft initiates the signal before picking 6 or 11.

Unable-to-release from the glider is illustration 10—do not swap it with the towplane’s cannot-release signal or unrelated speed/turn figures. Both “can’t release” signals exist; know which airframe sends which number.
Reduce-airspeed to the towplane is illustration 12 on the signal plate. Stop-ops (7) and glider can’t-release (10) are different emergencies—memorize 12 as the speed-change request.

Same reduce-airspeed cue: Figure 56 illustration 12 asks the towplane to slow. Keep it separate from stop (7) and can’t-release (10) so speed management does not get answered as an emergency release problem.
Towplane cannot release is illustration 8—mirror opposite of the glider’s can’t-release (10). Pick by which aircraft is signaling, not by “release” wording alone.

With the towplane still rolling and the glider airborne, crab into the wind to stay directly behind the towplane’s track—yaw-string/alignment behind the tug, not a wing-low bank that can yank the wing. Holding only “upwind rudder” without tracking behind the tug is incomplete.

Turning too early on aerotow pulls the glider’s nose toward the outside of the turn via towline tension—the tug is still going straight while you have already banked. Towplane nose pull or tug pitch-up are different geometry cues.

If the glider is up and the towplane loses power still on the runway, release immediately and clear to the left of the towplane so both have room. Landing straight ahead with spoilers or clearing right conflicts with the standard left clear-out.

After a towline break at low altitude, land straight ahead or use only slight turns to a suitable area—do not force a downwind 180 back to the runway. Wind-toward or wind-away turnbacks are the classic low-break trap.

A steep diving spiral is recovered by relaxing back-pressure and shallowing bank first, then gently raising the nose—pulling up while steeply banked tightens the spiral and raises load factor. More up-elevator plus aileron against overbank is the wrong sequence.

At min-sink in a thermal, a dropping inside wing is often the start of a stall/spin—use opposite rudder to slow the turn rate before grabbing aileron. Heavy opposite aileron at high AOA can worsen the drop; shove the nose only after yaw is controlled if needed.

In a spiral dive, airspeed and G loads rise with each turn; a spin holds roughly steady low speed and lower G with altitude loss per turn. Constant speed or little altitude loss points to a spin, not a spiral.

In gliders, forward slips for steepening the approach are normally flown with dive brakes or spoilers fully open so the slip adds drag without a big speed rise. Opposite rudder/aileron create the slip; “same-side” controls and ignoring spoilers are the usual wrong picks.

Getting low on XC: have a suitable landing area picked by about 2,000 feet AGL and a specific field by 1,500—do not press on course until 1,000 before planning. Denial until pattern altitude is the accident pattern this rule prevents.

Pushing ceilings/visibility to keep visual contact with terrain is called scud running—a classic VFR-into-IMC setup. Peer pressure and mindset are related ADM factors, but the maneuver itself is named scud running.
Anti-authority (“rules don’t apply here”) is reversed with the antidote “Follow the rules.” Match each hazardous attitude to its paired phrase—do not reuse macho or impulsivity antidotes.

Impulsivity (“do it quickly”) is countered by “Not so fast—think first.” Invulnerability’s antidote is different (“It could happen to me”), so read which attitude the stem names before picking the phrase.
Macho (“I can do it—watch this”) is reversed with “Taking chances is foolish.” “Nothing will happen” is invulnerability talk, not the macho antidote.
Resignation (“what’s the use”) is countered with “I am not helpless.” Blaming someone else keeps the resignation mindset; the antidote restores personal action.
Fitness for a given flight is the pilot’s go/no-go call under 61.53—even with a current medical. The FAA or AME does not make the day-of decision for you.

Most preventable accidents share human error as the common factor—not structural failure or pure mechanical surprise. ADM and hazardous-attitude antidotes exist to interrupt that chain before the flight.

Continuing VFR into IMC is the classic path to spatial disorientation and CFIT—without instruments or an IFR plan you lose reliable outside references fast. Do not confuse it with duck-under (descending below MDA/DH) or simply “getting behind” the airplane.

When repetitive flows live only in memory, checklists are the item pilots skip—short- and long-term memory both drop steps under distraction. Situation awareness and envelope awareness matter, but the neglected tool for recurring tasks is the written checklist.

Night passenger currency needs three full-stop takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days in the same category and class you will fly—not “any” aircraft and not type rating. Type is a narrower Part 61 term than category/class.

ATIS continuously broadcasts noncontrol airport/terminal information (weather, active runway, NOTAMs, etc.) at busy fields so you get the picture before calling ATC. It is not a terrain warning service and not “nonessential filler.”

Angle of attack is the acute angle between the chord line and the relative wind—the one that drives lift and stall. Angle of incidence is fixed in the airframe; dihedral is the upward wing slant for roll stability.

Bernoulli’s principle: faster flow over the curved upper surface lowers static pressure there, contributing to lift. Newton’s third law (action/reaction) and downward deflection of air are related ideas, but they are not Bernoulli.
Newton’s third law is action–reaction (equal and opposite). F=ma is the second law; conservation of energy is a different principle—do not mix the three on the exam.

As AOA changes, the center of pressure moves chordwise; that shift changes pitching moment, so aerodynamic balance and controllability change. It is not primarily a lift-coefficient or “lifting capacity” definition question.
Wake sinks behind a heavy jet: stay above its approach path all the way to touchdown and land beyond its touchdown point. Flying below or “2,000 ft behind and low” puts you into the vortices.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Each wingtip vortex rolls outward, upward, and around the tip (from behind: left wing clockwise, right counterclockwise). “Inward” is the usual wrong picture—do not reverse the sense of rotation.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Magnetic variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north (charted; east/west). Deviation is compass error from the airplane’s own magnetism/electronics—not the Earth-field offset.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: UNOS: turning from a southerly heading, the mag compass leads—shows the turn in the correct direction but faster than the real rate. From north it lags; do not pick the “initial turn opposite” (northerly) trap for a south start.

A motor-vehicle alcohol/drug action must be reported to the FAA no later than 60 days after the action—not 30 working days and not deferred until medical renewal. Clock starts on the MVA, not the next paperwork cycle.

For Experimental or Special light-sport certificates, FAA operating limitations travel with the special airworthiness certificate (Form 8130-7)—not buried in logbooks. Do not assume a standard AFM always holds them the way a normal-category airplane does.
Runway numbers are magnetic heading to the nearest 10°, dropped of the last digit—so 8 and 26 mean about 080° and 260° magnetic, not true, and not three-digit true like 008/026.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: The five hazardous attitudes are anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation—each with a memorized antidote. Broader phrases like “poor risk management” describe symptoms, not the five named attitudes.

ADM neutralization starts by recognizing the hazardous thought; only then do you apply the antidote and make a rational choice. “Recognizing invulnerability of the situation” garbles the invulnerability attitude itself.

ADM risk management leans on situational awareness, problem recognition, and good judgment to cut flight risk. That trio is the exam phrasing—do not swap it for the broader definition of decision-making alone.
Most midairs occur on clear days—good weather concentrates VFR traffic near airports and patterns, and complacency rises. Haze or night are not where the statistics peak.

links.label: AC 90-48 — Pilots’ Role in Collision Avoidance

details.summary: Meridians (longitude) run pole-to-pole and cross the Equator at right angles; they are not parallel to the Equator. The Greenwich line is 0° longitude, not latitude—common mix-up.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: True course → magnetic heading: east is least, west is best for variation, then apply wind correction (left WCA subtracts, right adds). The keyed path is add westerly variation and subtract a left wind-correction angle.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: When a part-time Class D tower closes, the D surface area goes away—airspace reverts to Class E and/or G as charted for those hours. Weather observers or ASOS do not keep it Class D by themselves.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Unless truncated by overlying controlled airspace, Class E goes up to—but not including—18,000 MSL, where Class A begins. 14,500 and 10,000 are common altitude traps from other rules, not the Class E ceiling.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Restricted airspace needs prior authorization from the using/controlling agency before you transit—filing IFR alone or calling a nearby base CO is not the rule. If hot and unauthorized, stay out.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: AIM practice: begin monitoring CTAF/UNICOM about 10 miles out at nontowered fields so you hear and announce in time. 20 or 25 miles is farther than the standard guidance.

An inbound destination sign (black background, yellow legend) points arriving traffic toward a destination on the field—terminal, cargo, military, etc. It is not a runway exit sign or a runway location sign.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: On the standard airport-sign figure set, the inbound destination sign is the black panel with yellow destination text/arrow (figure I)—same family as “directions for arriving aircraft.” Do not pick a yellow direction sign or a red runway sign.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: A taxiway direction sign is yellow with black taxiway letter(s) and arrow(s) showing where a taxiway turns or continues—figure K in the usual test plate. Location signs are black with yellow letters; do not swap them.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: A Convective SIGMET implies embedded thunderstorm hazards including turbulence at least moderate (and often severe)—treat the area as convective and hazardous. Do not downgrade it to “moderate storms over 30%” wording alone.

Local altimeter settings differ mainly because the surface heats unequally, creating pressure differences between stations—not because of terrain elevation or Coriolis by themselves. Set the current local altimeter so indicated altitude matches the pressure pattern you are flying in.

The RSA/OFZ boundary marking is the set of dashed yellow lines across a taxiway (figure G on the plate)—you are exiting the protected runway area. Do not confuse it with the solid/dashed runway hold short bars.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: A No Entry sign marks pavement aircraft must not use—wrong-way or prohibited movement area. It is not the “taxiway does not continue” array or the runway protected-area exit boundary.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Class D lateral limits are sized to contain the instrument procedures the controlled airspace protects—not a fixed 5 SM circle or a count of airports inside. Charted D outlines follow those approach needs.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: VFR gliders with a 4096-code transponder use 1202 for normal operation—not 1200 (powered VFR) or 7700 (emergency). Squawk 1202 unless ATC assigns another code.

When dialing a new squawk, avoid brushing through 7600—the lost-communications code that triggers ATC lost-comm handling. 7500 (hijack) and 7700 (emergency) are the other special codes to treat the same way.
The PIC owns the pre-takeoff passenger briefing—exits, belts, sterile expectations, emergency actions. Passengers and “a crewmember” do not relieve the pilot of that duty.

NALF Fentress (NFE) sits in Class E surface (or E starting at a depicted floor)—not the dashed-blue Class D ring and not uncontrolled G from the surface if E is charted. Read the sectional magenta/blue cues for that airport symbol.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Compass deviation comes from the aircraft’s own metals and electrical systems pulling the needle—corrected with a compass card. Variation is true-vs-magnetic Earth difference; northerly turning error is a dynamic dip error, not deviation.
Vehicle roadway markings are white dashed edge lines (and often a white dashed centerline) on the pavement—figure G on the test plate. Do not confuse them with runway or taxiway centerline stripes.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: A yellow demarcation bar spans the width ahead of a displaced threshold, separating that threshold from blast pad/stopway/taxiway pavement before the runway. It is not a taxiway hold line and does not itself mark the start of landing surface on the approach side.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Open an FSS briefing by stating whether the flight is VFR or IFR so the briefer scopes products and advisories correctly. Full name/address or a résumé of qualifications is not the required opener.

Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) are the go-to for regional GA forecast weather over a flight information region. Weather depiction and satellite are useful snapshots, but GFA is the forecast product named for that job.

Aviation Advisory Circulars are obtained via the FAA website (or the AC checklist process)—not by asking an FBO and not by reading the AIM. Free vs paid depends on the AC; the distribution path is still FAA.

Altimeter settings differ between stations mainly because unequal solar heating creates regional pressure differences. Terrain elevation and Coriolis affect other weather processes—they are not the exam cause of setting variation.

On a sectional, tick marks on the latitude/longitude neatlines let you plot 47°35'30"N, 100°43'00"W—that fix is Makeeff in the figure area. Measure carefully; nearby airports sit only minutes of arc away.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Plot 47°21'N, 101°01'W on the sectional neatlines to identify Washburn—not the neighboring Johnson or Lorentzen symbols. Latitude first (north scale), then longitude (west scale).

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: From the cockpit, marking G (yellow RSA/OFZ dashed boundary behind you as you exit) confirms you are on the runway and about to clear into the taxiway. It is not a taxiway hold-short cue for entering the runway.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Sign E is a taxiway location sign—black background with yellow “B”—confirming you are already on taxiway B. Yellow-background signs with arrows are direction signs ahead; do not treat a location sign as a hold-area warning.

links.label: AIM — Airport Marking Aids and Signs

details.summary: Class D width is built around the instrument approaches that need protected airspace, so the charted ring or polygon follows those procedures. A blanket 5 SM radius or airport-count rule is the distractor.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Airports charted “NO SVFR” (here Dallas-Fort Worth International and Dallas Love Field) ban fixed-wing Special VFR. Other metro airports on the same plate may still allow SVFR—read the notation, not the city name alone.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Norfolk International is Class C: you need an operating Mode C (altitude-encoding) transponder and two-way radio to land/take off there. DME or a VOR receiver is not the Class C equipment pair on this question.

links.label: FAA VFR sectional / chart users guide

details.summary: Part-time Class D exists only while the tower is operating; after close it reverts to Class E and/or G as published. ASOS/observers do not preserve D, and the designation does change with the hours.

In aerotow turns, match the towplane’s bank and point the glider’s nose at the towplane’s outside (high) wingtip so you stay outside the tow’s turn radius. Aiming at the inside tip or straight at the fuselage cuts inside and slack/rope issues follow.
METAR remark RAB35 means rain began at 35 minutes past the hour; with a 1800Z observation that is 1835Z. It is not barometer +0.35 or “blowing mist” visibility code.
